messages.subject_clean: compiling doc PDFs w/o Lucida fonts
messages.body_plain:
You should be able to compile using Computer Modern
and Times fonts by just removing the lucimatx
include package and including packages times and
amssymb.

These are the first includepackages in the
tex file, so I highlighted how to do this and
added instructions at the top of gm.tex.

I like the x-height and "color" balance of
Lucida Bright serif and Lucida Sans Typewriter
typewriter font.  I really like the latter (it's
what I use in the shell and in Emacs, though
on the Mac I've been using Menlo, which is close).

I really hate the Courier font built into Tex.
And there doesn't seem to be a bold courier built
into computer modern, but there is in Times Roman.

This should also make Andrew happy in that our doc
won't look like every other Times or Computer Modern
LaTeX doc out there.

- Bob

messages.subject: Eigen-decomposition-based covariance-matrix transforms?
messages.body_plain:
I finally got my head around the LKJ transform
as specified in terms of Cholesky factors by Ben.
I'm still blown away that the CPCs generate a
correlation matrix when all the dust settles.

Having just boned up on positive definiteness,
it appears another way to specify a covariance
matrix is through an Eigen decomposition in
terms of a set of K orthonormal vectors and
K positive ordered Eigenvalues.  We already have
the data type and transform for the Eigenvalues.

Conceptually, we should be able to generate a
set of orthonormal vectors by

    choose normal x[1] from R^K
    choose normal x[2] from (K-1)-dim null space of { x[1] }
    choose normal x[3] from (K-2)-dim null space of { x[1], x[2] }
    ...

Is there an efficient way to do that without
running solvers?  For instance, in 3D, generating
the first vector is easy, with

   x[1,1]^2 in +/- (0,1)

   x[1,2]^2 in +/- (0,1 - x[1,1]^2)

   x[1,3]^2 = 1 - x[1,1]^2 - x[1,2]^2

x[2,] is then constrained so that

      1 = x[2,]' * x[2,]

and

      0 = x[1,]' * x[2,]

So we have to choose an x[2,1] that ensures the above
is solvable (basically, the absolute value of
x[1,1] * x[2,1] can't be too large so that the remaining
coordinates can't bring the solution back to 0 while
retaining unit length).

Then once we choose x[2,1], the values x[2,2] and x[2,3]
will be solvable for because of the unit-length constraint.
Then x[3,] is fully determined by the unit-length constraint.
That leaves (K choose 2) free parameters in total,
plus K eigenvalue parameters.

- Bob

P.S.  In the current setup, we can use the cov_matrix
transform to define all sorts of priors on covariance
matrices.  For example, we could put a prior on the
positive ordered sequence of Eigenvalues.  One way to
do this is choose the smallest Eigenvalue, the condition
[ratio of largest to smallest], then fill in the ones
in between choosing uniformly on the remaining interval.

messages.body_plain:
Hey Bob,

I don't know anything about this LKJ transform, could you send along a reference?  Google seems to have failed me on that one.

At any rate, a couple things came to mind for representing orthonormal vectors for covariance matrices.

1. Grahm-Schmidt orthogonalization on a set of non-orthonormal vectors

2. Ignore orthogonality and just take use a set of vectors.  The odds of n randomly chosen vectors actually being linearly dependent is small.  (This approach is taken in, e.g., collaborative filtering problems where enforcing the orthonormal constraint is expensive and/or hard.)

3. Use the skew-symmetric representation of the tangent space or orthogonal matrices.  The mapping to an orthogonal matrix is then the matrix exponential of a skew-symmetric matrix.  See http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skew-symmetric_matrix#Infinitesimal_rotations

4.  (Shameless self plug) Implement non-linearly constrained HMC.  See http://www.cs.toronto.edu/~mbrubake/projects/cmcmc/  If I ever get some more free time, I might implement this myself and would be happy to help someone else implement it.  There are even some clever specializations one could do for orthogonality constraints.  It would be a decidedly unique feature for stan.

Those ideas aside, is there a reason to replace the Cholesky factor based representation?  It seems easy to implement and has some advantages when computing elliptical distributions which would need the Cholesky factors anyway.

Cheers,
Marcus

>

> Cholesky factors.  Ben also has a note he sent me earlier with
> more details.  That should probably at least be made into
> an Arxiv paper to cite in our doc.
>
>
> > At any rate, a couple things came to mind for representing orthonormal
> > vectors for covariance matrices.
> >
> > 1. Grahm-Schmidt orthogonalization on a set of non-orthonormal vectors
>
> I thought of that, but isn't there a problem because
> the orthogonalization is many to one?  I've never done
> non-bijective transforms, but hey, I had never done any
> before last year.

Yes, it would make computing the log-determinant of the jacobian impossible as the Jacobian would be rectangular.

>
>
> > 2. Ignore orthogonality and just take use a set of vectors.  The odds of
> > n randomly chosen vectors actually being linearly dependent is small.
> > (This approach is taken in, e.g., collaborative filtering problems where
> > enforcing the orthonormal constraint is expensive and/or hard.)
>
> Approach 1. would rely on this feature, too.
>
> Don't the linearly dependent vectors have measure zero among
> all the sets of vectors?

Almost, the set of nxn singular matrices is of measure zero.  A set of n n-dimensional vectors is almost certain to a) be somewhat linearly dependent and b) still span the full space.  b) is just a restatement of the measure zero argument.  a) follows by considering that, with n-1 orthonormal vectors, there are exactly 2 choices of the last vector, which must have measure zero.

>
>
> > 3. Use the skew-symmetric representation of the tangent space or
> > orthogonal matrices.  The mapping to an orthogonal matrix is then the
> > matrix exponential of a skew-symmetric matrix.  See
> > http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skew-symmetric_matrix#Infinitesimal_rotations
>
> Thanks -- hadn't seen that.  We'll see if I can
> understand it.

In 3D this is called the exponential map representation of rotations which might help with intuition.

Basically, you represent an n dimensional orthonormal matrix as an n(n − 1)/2-dimensional vector whose entries comprise the off diagonal entries of the skew-symmetric matrix.  The magnitude of the vector is the angle of the rotation and the direction of the vector is the axis of rotation.  This is a minimal representation of O(n), but has singularities when the magnitude is zero or a multiple of 2pi.  These are almost unavoidable (see hairy ball theorem) and rarely a problem in practice, but can come up.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
So anyone with a 32-bit Windows machine will
be out of luck trying to compile multivariate
models at -O3.  We just watched it crash at the 2GB
mark, which is all 32-bit hardware supports in
terms of process size (the OS/motherboard reserves
the other 2GB of potential address space).

The key to using less space in the compiler is
cutting down on the size of our translation units.
That doesn't play nicely with all of our header-only
template libs (Boost, Eigen, and the way we currently
have Stan organized).

I'm pretty sure it's possible to refactor the parser.
There are examples in the Boost parser doc:

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_49_0/libs/spirit/example/qi/compiler_tutorial/

I haven't been able to refactor the parser so that
it uses explicit instantiation rather than being
header only.  There's a simple working example of how to
do explicit instantiation with doc in

     src/demo/templ_inst_demo

So far, I can't get it to link.  The refactoring of the
grammars is in the subdirectory

     stan/gm/grammars

I just added a couple of files that aren't being
used:

     src/stan/gm/ast_header_def_unused_attempt.hpp
     src/stan/gm/ast_header_unused_attempt.hpp

in which I tried to refactor the abstract
syntax tree (the data structure created by the parser
to represent a Stan program).

I can compile .o files, but I can't link.  Rather than duplicate
defs, I get missing defs this time.  I think it may
have something to do with the remaining templates in
ast.hpp, which could either be explicitly instantiated
during compilation with another file like the .cpp files
in the stan/gm/grammars directory or
replaced with their instantiations directly in the code.

- Bob

Let me try to explain.

C and C++ compilation involves two stages:

   1.  Building one or more relocatable object files (.o)

       > clang++ -c foo.cpp
       > ls foo.o

       > clang++ -c bar.cpp
       > ls bar.o

   2.  Linking the relocatable object files into an executable:

       > clang++ foo.o bar.o -o myprog
       > ls myprog

The unit through which a relocatable object file is
built is called a "translation unit".  In the first
example, that's the contents of "foo.cpp", with all of
the (recursive) includes folded in.   In the second, it's
the same for "bar.cpp".

Now, to achieve this, we need to split definitions and
declarations.

A.  Declaration (traditionally in a .h file)
     int foo(int x);

B.  Definition (traditionally in a .c file)
     int foo(int x) { return x + 1; }

In order to generate relocatable object files, we only need
the declarations of functions/variables on which we depend.

Here's the key:

    In order to link, every function and constant needs to be
    DEFINED in EXACTLY ONE of the .o files.

Templates mess all of this up.  They're halfway between
declarations and definitions.  It's only when you specify the
type for a template that you get a definition (or declaration).

So template libs, like Eigen and Boost, are often what's
called "header only", meaning that they put the declarations
and definitions in a single file and everything gets built
as one big translation unit.

That's what Stan does now.  For instance, the following
does both the compilation and linking:

    > clang++ baz.cpp -o myprog

but it requires baz to import DEFINITIONS of everything
it needs (other than the std libs, which presumably get
linked in as necessary).

The header guards on the .hpp files make sure that each
item is only defined once.

So what we want to do is break the parser and perhaps
the models into pieces, one with a declaration, and one
with a definition.

Because templates don't have a definition until they're
instantiated, C++ lets you create a third type of file called
a template instantiation file.  This is usually a .cpp
file that indicates which instantiations of the templates
you want.  It then plays the role of the definition file,
getting compiled separately and then linked in later against
a .o file compiled by including only the declarations.

The simplest way to understand this in action is to look
at the example in:

    stan/src/demo/templ_inst_demo

where I provide a very simple textbook example.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: covariance-matrix transforms?
messages.body_plain:
Bob's post about parameterizing a covariance matrix in terms of a decomposition raises another point that I had been meaning to bring up.

If Sigma is an unknown KxK covariance matrix, then it has a Cholesky decomposition

Sigma = L * L'

where L is lower-triangular with positive diagonal entries. Conversely, for any such L, L * L' is a valid covariance matrix.

So, Stan could simply parameterize a covariance matrix in terms of the K choose 2 strictly lower-triangular elements of L --- which are unconstrained --- and the K diagonal elements of L, which are unconstrained aside from needing to be positive. At the moment, Stan does *not* do that, but we could, particularly if the user wants to place a {scaled, inverse} Wishart prior on Sigma. Conversely, it would be very difficult to specify a prior on the unbounded parameters and understand what that implies for Sigma.

What Stan actually does at the moment is to write

Sigma = D * L * L' * D

where D is a diagonal matrix of standard deviations and L is parameterized in terms of so-called canonical partial correlations (CPCs) such that L * L' is a correlation matrix. Furthermore, we use exp() to form a positive standard deviation from an unbounded parameter and tanh() to bind a CPC to the (-1,1) interval from an unbounded parameter. In other words, that entails three more levels of transformation that are not strictly necessary and are in fact wasteful if the user wants to place a {scaled, inverse} Wishart prior on Sigma.

The motivation for the extra three levels of transformation --- and the ultimate contribution of the LKJ paper --- is that you can write the joint density of a correlation matrix in a simple, useful way:

f(L(eta) * L(eta)' | eta) = constant * det[ L(eta) * L(eta)' ]^(eta - 1)

where eta > 0 is a hyperprior that affects the shape of the density for each CPC. This gives you a firm basis for specifying a prior on a correlation matrix: Iff eta = 1, then the joint density is constant and all correlation matrices are equally likely,  and as eta -> oo, L(eta) * L(eta)' has to converge to the identity matrix. And it is pretty easy to supplement this with a prior on the standard deviations to imply (with an easy change-of-variables) a prior on a covariance matrix.

I think that is a substantively better way to specify a prior on a covariance matrix, but certainly the {scaled, inverse} Wishart priors are more popular because they were the only practical choices until a few years ago. So, if a user is going to use a {scaled, inverse} Wishart prior on Sigma, is it worth our coding effort to provide a simpler parameterization in terms of the lower-triangular elements of L? I'd say probably. And to get back to Bob's question, is there any other decomposition of a covariance matrix that is both computationally efficient and lends itself to specifying reasonable priors? Not that I know of, which is why I'd say to wait on that until a situation presents itself where an alternate decomposition is necessary.

Ben

I don't see an easy route. One could impose the constraint that the i-th diagonal element is 1.0 minus the sum of squares of the elements of L in that row, but sometimes the sum of squares will randomly be greater than 1.0, in which case you would have to bounce. The miracle of the LKJ transform is that this sum of squares can be represented as the transformation from hyperspherical coordinates with a radius of 1.0.

> How should we build data types into Stan to support
> LKJ?  We can now separate the issue from that of specifying
> a basic covariance matrix transform.

Well, if we went whole hog to a CovMatrix class in C++, we could define some publicly accessible flags that the constructor would set indicating "how" this covariance matrix came to be (plain Cholesky, LKJ, AR1, eigendecomposition, whatever) in addition to having all the ingredients to represent the covariance matrix (and its inverse) in a myriad of different ways that may be favorable depending on the calculation.

If we don't go whole hog to a CovMatrix class, then we somehow need to figure out from the .stan file if the user wants a LKJ prior and in that case, we need to do the more complicated LKJ transform. Ergo, I don't like this route as much.

> Any suggestions for a name?  Then we could use multivariate
> densities defined directly in terms of Cholesky factors,
> which should be much speedier as Ben's pointed out before.

If there were a CovMatrix class and multivariate densities were defined for a CovMatrix (as opposed to a Matrix that happens to be a covariance matrix), then the density could figure out whatever it needs (often just the Cholesky factor), check whether the things it needs have been initialized (and if not, calculate and cache them), and proceed to calculate the log density.

> >
> > f(L(eta) * L(eta)' | eta) = constant * det[ L(eta) * L(eta)' ]^(eta - 1)
> >
> > where eta > 0 is a hyperprior that affects the shape of the density for
> > each CPC.
>
> What is L(eta) here?

I just mean that L is a function of eta. Specifically, L is a function of the CPCs, and the shape parameters for the beta prior on each CPC are a function of eta.

In the simpler parameterization where

Sigma = L * L'

L is not a function of anything (except for the diagonal elements which are the antilog of something), so there is less for the computer to do. Although, we do need to code up the Jacobian for the transformation from the lower triangle of L to the lower triangle of Sigma.

messages.body_plain:
That will teach me not to read the code first, I had assumed that Stan was using the L * L' representation of a covariance matrix.

So I think this discussion is conflating two different issues/use cases:

1. Someone wants to define a covariance matrix for use in a model in arbitrary or yet to be determined ways.
2. Someone wants to specify a prior in terms of the LKJ representation, the cholesky factorization, the eigenvalue decomposition or some other arbitrary representation of the covariance matrix.

1 means the covariance matrix is primal and how it's used is arbitrary or unpredictable.  Hence we want the simplest, most compact and efficient way to represent a (positive definite) covariance matrix.  Here it seems the L * L' form with a log transformation on the diagonal is the most sensible.

2 on the other hand means that from a covariance matrix we'll need to compute things which may be inconvenient or expensive and we may just want to represent the covariance matrix directly in those terms.

For me it seems that there should be different types for these cases in the Stan modelling language.  A basic definition of a cov_matrix corresponds to use case 1.  The LKJ form could be handled with a corr_matrix type and vector which is constrained to have positive elements and the user would define a transformed parameter for the full covariance.  The Cholesky case, the eigenvalue case and anything else could be handled similarly.

An example showing three different representations to make things clear:

parameters {
  cov_matrix<N> Sigma_basic;

  corr_matrix<N> Sigma_LKJ_correlations;
  vector<N> Sigma_LKJ_logstddevs; // or add some way to make the entries positive

  chol_factor<N> Sigma_cholesky_L;
}

transformed parameters {
  matrix<N,N> Sigma_LKJ;
  matrix<N,N> Sigma_cholesky;

  Sigma_LKJ <- lkj_covariance_matrix(Sigma_LKJ_correlations,exp(Sigma_LKJ_logstddevs));
  Sigma_cholesky <- Sigma_cholesky_L * Sigma_cholesky_L';
}

model {
  x1 ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma_basic);
  lp__ <- lp__ + arbitrary_sigma_prior(Sigma_basic,...); // or whatever

  x2 ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma_LKJ);
  Sigma_LKJ_correlations ~ lkj_corr_prior(...);

  x3 ~  multi_normal(mu,Sigma_cholesky); // or multi_normal_chol(mu,Sigma_cholesky_L);
  Sigma_cholesky_L ~ inverse_wishart_chol(...);

  Etc.
}

In other words, if someone wants an LKJ prior, then they can define their model appropriately.

It places a somewhat larger burden on the user but avoids having to add heuristics to determine which representation to use based on how the model is specified which just seems ugly.  However, if the user knows they want an LKJ prior, then presumably they know what the LKJ representation means, at least in terms of a correlation matrix and standard deviations.

Adding a CovMatrix class makes it possible to speed some things up automatically under the hood, but would still require deciding how best to represent the covariance matrix for a given model.  That would mean the same kind of heuristics or some kind of hinting in the .stan file provided by the user.

Cheers,
Marcus

L_is_initialized
Sigma_inverse
Sigma_inverse_is_initialized
L_inverse
L_inverse_is_initialized
eigenvalues
eigenvalues_are_initialized
eigenvectors
eigenvectors_are_initialized
determinant
determinant_is_calculated
transformation_scheme
...

The density function (or whatever function is downstream) could first check whether what it wants has been initialized. If not, initialize it. Then, calculate the return value.

So, for example, the multi_log function would test L_inverse_is_initialized, and in many cases, it wouldn't be. Then, test whether L_is_initialized, and in many cases, it would be. (If not, Sigma should have been initialized, so Cholesky decompose it and update L and L_is_initialized). Forward solve L to get L_inverse, cache it, and change L_inverse_is_initialized. Test determinant_is_calculated and if that fails, calculate and cache the determinant of Sigma from L. Now you have all the pieces to evaluate the density. And, moreover, everything is ready in case this CovMatrix needs to be used again (i.e., you need to evaluate the density for the next observation).

In short, we could have fewer verbosely named functions and allow each density function to figure out what they need from the CovMatrix class.

Ben

> Speaking as a user, my first goal is to be able to fit multilevel models with the scaled-inverse-Wishart class of priors with dimension up to, say, 10 or so.  But I'm sure I'll have other goals once that gets working!

The dimensionality is not a major issue for the proposed code refactoring as far as I can tell. But the dimensionality is relevant to whether a chosen prior is reasonable (which Andrew knows well because we co-wrote a paper with a couple of other people about how scaled-inverse-Wishart with dimensionality > 2 and low degrees of freedom puts more mass in the corners of the parameter space where covariance matrices are nearly singular). The {scaled, inverse} Wishart priors are overly popular due to their computational convenience in Gibbs samplers, but I suspect they are computationally inconvenient for HMC due to the induced high dependence among parameters. Maybe NUTS 3 will make this feasible, but it should already be feasible in NUTS 1 with an LKJ prior and eta >= 1.

> I think we're in agreement: a cov_matrix defaults to a Cholesky factor parameterization, and other forms can be

> So in summary, this is proposing to add a chol_factor and corr_matrix type to the modeling language.  Beyond that maybe
> also a way to specify a vector of positive reals?  The CovMatrix class can be added somewhat independently of this.

The currently supported types (arranged by ISA/assignability)
are:

   matrix(M,N)
       cov_matrix(K)
       corr_matrix(K)
   row_vector(N)
   vector(M)
       simplex(K)
       pos_ordered(K)
   real
       real(lb,)
       real(,ub)
       real(lb,ub)
   int
       int(lb,)
       int(,ub)
       int(lb,ub)

plus arrays of arbitrary dimensions with entries
declared to be any of these types.  Stan doesn't
currently forbid

   cov_matrix(4) Sigma;
   matrix(4,4) M;
   ...
   Sigma <- M;

but every use case is checked (though not at
intermediate stages of processing).

There's not a positive vector type, but there is
a positive array of reals declared with lb = 0.
We could add bounds to the basic matrix, row vector
and vector types.

Three new types of square matrices are under discussion:

       symmetric_matrix(K)
       triangular_matrix(K)
           cov_matrix_cholesky(K)

and a new vector for points on the unit
hypersphere:

       hypersphere(K)

I'm about to reparameterize cov_matrix using the
Cholesky factors.

I've also thought some typedefs would be useful:

    typedef real(0,) positive;
    typedef real(0,1) probability;
    typedef real(-1,1) correlation;
    typedef int(0,)  natural;
    typedef int(0,1) binary;

I'm pretty sure we can handle correlation matrices
by using first a bound and then a hyperspherical
transform on the rows so that the sum of the square
entries is 1.  That'll get us positive-definiteness
and a unit diagonal.  All other entries must have
absolute values below 1 because they're all products
of unit vectors and only the diagonals are from
ones going in the same direction.  I think I got
my geometrical reasoning right:  if x and y are
unit-length vectors, then

    x' * x  >=  x' * y  >=  x' * -x

- Bob

I put the derivation of the transform and unconstrained
transform with absolute Jacobian determinant into the

The punchline is that the transform involves:

    - K exponential functions,

and its log absolute Jacobian determinant involves:

    - 1 + K + (K * K) additions

Cholesky factor product?  I'm afraid it'll be
O(K^3) like ordinary matrix products, but was hoping
all the missing terms reduced the order.  The logs
and exponents will probably dominate at low orders (K < 20)
anyway.

then you'll have to follow the instructions
at the very top of gm.tex and do a little editing to get
it to run pdflatex with built-in Times Roman + AMS Fonts.
I don't know if there's a legal, free way to get the
Lucida fonts installed.  I went with the $99 package
a while back when I was writing a manual for our company.

A corollary of the idea to parameterize

Sigma = L * L'

without the user knowing it, is that we could often specify L^(-1) directly instead of first specifying L and then inverting it with Eigen's forward solve algorithm. L^(-1) is what we need for an ellipical distribution and it has the same properties as L: Unrestricted cells in the strict lower triangle, positive cells on the diagonal, and zero in the strict upper triangle.

The user may want to store the posterior distribution of Sigma, in which case we would have to calculate [L^(-1)]^(-1) = L and then L * L'. But, we could do that after casting L^(-1) from var to double, so we wouldn't have to calculate a zillion auto-diffs.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: puzzles regarding cov matrix models
messages.body_plain:
(replying inline to stan-dev so that everyone can follow)

On Wed, Apr 4, 2012 at 11:17 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> Ben
>
> That's interesting, thanks for sending.  The pictures are pretty.  Usually I don't get much from 3d scatterplots but these really work!
>
> The inv-Wishart with d+1 df gives uniform marginals on the corrs, but I can see how, to get the uniform marginal [sic, AG meant joint], you have to pile up mass on the corners.  One solution would be to increase the df, right?

Yes. The expectation of the inverse Wishart is S / (d - k - 1) iff d > k + 1. So, I picked the popular but extreme case that the expectation doesn't exist. Calculating the expectation of an implied correlation is a bit involved, but as d increases, the standard deviation of the correlations shrinks.

library(MCMCpack)
k <- 3
I <- diag(k)
mark <- lower.tri(I, diag = FALSE)
REPS <- 10000
dof <- (k+1):20
results <- sapply(dof, FUN = function(d) replicate(REPS, cov2cor(riwish(d, I))[mark]) )
colnames(results) <- dof
plot(dof, apply(results, 2, sd), type = "l", xlab = "Degrees of freedom",
     ylab = "Standard deviation of correlations")

However, I continue to think that increasing the shape parameter of a LKJ distribution (starting at eta = 1 -> joint uniform) is more intuitive than increasing the degrees of freedom of an inverse Wishart (starting at d = k + 1 -> no moments) in part because the "degrees of freedom" is kind of a nondescript number, while the LKJ correlation matrix is a composition of independent symmetric betas on (-1,1) whose shape parameters are a function of eta.

> More fundamentally, though, we don't have a great way of thinking about these multivariate models.  Once d>2, I have very little intuition about what sorts of models would make sense.  Maybe the joint uniform is fine, I just can't get my head around what would be the best parameterization.

I think what you said is generally true: Most people don't have a good understanding of joint distributions, correlation matrices, etc. and even if they understand them, they don't have strong priors about correlation matrices, particularly if it is a correlation matrix among parameters rather than data. So, in that situation, a joint uniform distribution on a correlation matrix accurately reflects their prior beliefs. And insofar as they have informative prior beliefs, they probably slightly favor the identity matrix over the nearly singular correlation matrices, which can be accomplished with an eta slightly greater than 1.0.

> A related issue is that in a multilevel model, if you shift the x-variables (for example, by centering them), this changes all the correlations.

Yes, if the correlation matrix in question is among parameters.

> Based on what you're saying here, the uniform on the corrs does seem to make the most sense.  Is there a parameterized version of this (just as the inv-wishart has that df parameterization)?

Yes, what Bob and I call the LKJ distribution over a correlation matrix (with shape parameter eta > ) in stan is based on this paper

http://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=5449838284935626139&hl=en&as_sdt=0,33

which gives conditions under which the PDF of a correlation matrix is

f(Sigma | eta) = 1 / c(k,eta) * det(Sigma)^(eta - 1)

where Sigma is a correlation matrix (and a function of eta) and c(k,eta) only depends on k and eta. And so eta = 1 -> f(Sigma | eta) = 1 / c(k,eta) is constant.

> Also, getting back to the uniform model (which I think was also discussed by Barnard, Meng, and McCulloch), let's think briefly about high dimensions.  I know that earlier I said I'm only interested in d up to 10, but it would be good to understand the limit of very high dimensions, if only to get a sense of what the model is doing.  If d is high, then the joint uniform distribution on the corrs implies a marginal dist on each corr that is concentrated near 0.  There's a conceptual problem with such a model:  imagine you start with two variables, y1 and y2, with a corr rho_12 which has a uniform prior.  Now we add more and more variables:  y3, y4, y5, etc.  If we go with the inverse-Wishart, we're fine, all these models are coherent (although they have other problems, as you've noted!).  But if we go with the joint uniform, then adding y3, y4, y5, etc. has the effect of changing the prior on rho_12.  Which doesn't seem right to me, somehow, that the addition of more variables into the analysis changes the model for an existing variable.  This sort of paradox shoudn't stop us from possibly using the model, but I'd like to have a good way of thinking about it.

I don't think it is a problem with the prior; it is a problem with high dimensions. An earlier paper by Joe

http://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=8483085447913922429&hl=en&as_sdt=0,33

proves that the c(k,eta) term in the PDF when eta = 1 is

c(k) = c(k - 1) * 2^(k^2 - 2 * k + 1) * Beta(k/2,k/2)^(k - 1)

where Beta() is the Beta function. The hypervolume of correlation matrices is c(k), which eventually starts to decrease as Beta(k/2,k/2)^(k - 1) shrinks faster than 2^(k^2 - 2 * k + 1) increases:

k     c(k)
2     2.0
3     4.934802
4     11.69731
5     22.53256
6     31.11388
7     27.85823
8     14.87740
9     4.411544
10   0.682269

So, given that correlation matrices must be positive definite, as k increases, a Bayesian robot should update its beliefs about the correlations to make them closer to zero. In other words, for large k, the set of correlation matrices is small relative to the set of merely symmetric matrices with ones on the diagonal, and the correlation matrices in that set tend to have small off-diagonals. But people are not Bayesian robots and can fall into the trap of thinking that their model stays "the same" as k increases, instead of conditioning their prior beliefs on the known k.

Ben

On Apr 4, 2012, at 4:17 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:

> <covariance.png>
> Here is a demonstration as to why I think scaled inverse Wishart priors are going to be problematic with HMC, relative to scaled LKJ priors. This is similar to some of the plots in that paper Andrew and I did, except here I am only doing 3 dimensions. Higher dimensions have the same intuition but are harder to visualize. In every case, I draw 10,000 times from a distribution, and plot the sampling distribution of some quantity. For inverse Wishart, I always use identity scale and 4 degrees of freedom. For LKJ, I always set the shape parameter equal to 1.0, so that the correlation matrix has a joint uniform distribution.
>
> In the top left, I rescale the inverse Wishart covariance matrix into a correlation matrix and plot the three correlations. The main point here is that rarely would anyone have a prior belief that places so much mass in the corners of this constrained space. In contrast (top right), in many situations, people do not have strong prior beliefs about a correlation matrix, so a joint uniform accurately reflects their ignorance.
>
> [sic, BG messed up the indices: It should be L_{21}, L_{31}, and L_{32}]
>
> In the bottom left, I take the Cholesky decomposition of an inverse Wishart covariance matrix and plot L_{12}, L_{13}, and L_{23}. This is the unconstrained space (ignoring the diagonal) that stan would be drawing from, and its tails are scary. I had to blow up all the axes just to hold the occasional extreme points.
>
> In the LKJ case, we do not actually draw from an unconstrained L, but in the bottom right, I plot L_{12}, L_{13}, and L_{23} anyway where L * L' is a jointly uniform correlation matrix. If we were drawing from this unconstrained space, it doesn't look like it would be a big problem, and this intuition carries over to the unconstrained space we are actually drawing from in the LKJ case.
>
> To summarize, the popular scaled inverse Wishart parameterization
>
> Sigma = S * W * S
>
> where S is a diagonal matrix and W has an inverse Wishart distribution is similar in form to the unpopular scaled LKJ parameterization
>
> Sigma = D * (L * L') * D
>
> where D is a diagonal matrix of standard deviations and L * L' is a correlation matrix (often with a uniform distribution).
>
> The main differences are:
>
> 1) D has well-defined standard deviations on its diagonal, whereas S has weird positive numbers that are not standard deviations and harder to form a marginal prior over.
>
> 2) Few understand the inverse Wishart distribution and fewer genuinely believe it reflects their priors over a covariance matrix, whereas many people can understand what it means to draw uniformally from the set of all correlation matrices and in many cases that reflects their well-founded prior ignorance over a correlation matrix.
>
> 3) The unconstrained space that corresponds to the constrained space for an inverse Wishart is computationally scary, whereas the unconstrained space --- the atanh() of symmetric betas on (-1,1) with shape parameter >= 1.0 --- that corresponds to the constrained space for a jointly uniform correlation matrix is pretty tame.
>
> In short, with a scaled inverse Wishart prior, you have to get bailed out by the data or fiddle with the degrees of freedom parameter. But again, it is more straightforward to fiddle with the shape parameter for the LKJ prior: Starting from eta = 1.0, increasing eta puts more mass on the identity matrix and less mass in the corners of the constrained space.
>
> Ben
>
>

messages.subject: dot_product and bernoulli_logit
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I went ahead and implemented a vectorized version of the dot_product()
function for arrays (it's in stan/agrad/matrix.hpp). In an informal
test, it seems to be around 25x faster than the old version, so if
you're doing anything that can be expressed as a dot product you
should probably be using the vectorized version.

Also, I was unsatisfied with the domain errors that I was getting when
trying to test moderately large (i.e., O(100)) values for predictors
in logistic regressions, so I implemented bernoulli_logit_log(), which
is equivalent to bernoulli_log(inv_logit(theta)) except that it can
handle large values of theta (e.g., abs(theta) > 20) correctly.

So, when implementing a logistic regression in Stan, I recommend
replacing code that looks like this:

    temp <- 0;
    for (d in 1:D)
      temp <- temp + beta[d] * x[n, d];
    y[n] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(temp));

with code that looks like this:

    y[n] ~ bernoulli_logit(dot_product(beta, x[n]));

It's safer and faster.

Matt

the dump format that stan uses for reads.

it writes the dimensions as "2:3", whereas if you
dump out a 2x4 matrix, it writes it as "c(2,4)".
I didn't write Stan's dump reader generally enough

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] bernoulli_logit and log1p_exp()
messages.body_plain:
Hmm. Maybe we should have only one implementation of log1p_exp(),
since the difference between

log(1/(1+exp(-a))) = -log(1 + exp(-a))

and

log(1 + exp(a))

is only a couple of minus signs. Then again, if we expect
bernoulli_logit_log() to be called enough then the couple-of-percent
performance gain from rolling those minus signs into the adjoint
calculation is maybe worth it.

On the subject of implementation details, I believe that using

if (a < -20)
     return exp(a);

will produce more accurate results than

if (a < -20)
     return 0;

since log(1 + exp(-20)) is in fact (very slightly) greater than 0.
(This is probably not important very often, but sometimes there's a
big difference between 0 and 2e-9.) The approximation comes from
taking a 1st-order Taylor approximation of log() around 1.

Matt

That's what I was thinking.  But the other difference
is that you're pre-unfolding the Taylor expansion here.
In general, we want to keep going with these unfoldings
to the extent that the extra code difficulty (affecting
comprehensibility and hence maintainability) is worth it.

For logistic regression, I'm thinking every little bit will help.
Of course, those - will get dwarfed if the dimensionality of
the predictors is high, as the other e-mail thread's been
pointing out.

The outer - is free because it's in a log_prob -= x
context, and it has to be a plus or a minus.

We could also add a log(1+exp(-a)) function :-)
It's going to require some discipline to choose the right
boundary here for unfolding and building in new expressions.

Ideally, we could do some of this with expression templates
that would convert log(1 + exp(a)) to log1p_exp(a) behind
the scenes.

> big difference between 0 and 2e-9.) The approximation comes from

My bad.  I just put in the wrong boundary in a
cut-and-paste braino.  The bound's more like -800 or so:

    if (a < -800) return 0;

Below -800, double-precision exp underflows to 0
and the whole thing reduces to log(1) = 0.

We just need to make sure the gradient doesn't
also disappear!

- Bob

P.S.  I knew -O3 is the way Matt rolls (quoting him from
       a way-back e-mail message).  I just wanted to make
       sure everyone else was.   Daniel was surprised how
       much of a difference it made in running our entire
       set of BUGS models for the model regression (not the stats
       sense) test.  It can easily be a factor of 10 in some
       of the cases we're looking at.  We leaned very heavily on
       compiler optimizations to keep the code cleaner.

On Apr 5, 2012, at 2:01 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:

>
> Yes. The expectation of the inverse Wishart is S / (d - k - 1) iff d > k + 1. So, I picked the popular but extreme case that the expectation doesn't exist. Calculating the expectation of an implied correlation is a bit involved, but as d increases, the standard deviation of the correlations shrinks.
>
> library(MCMCpack)
> k <- 3
> I <- diag(k)
> mark <- lower.tri(I, diag = FALSE)
> REPS <- 10000
> dof <- (k+1):20
> results <- sapply(dof, FUN = function(d) replicate(REPS, cov2cor(riwish(d, I))[mark]) )
> colnames(results) <- dof
> plot(dof, apply(results, 2, sd), type = "l", xlab = "Degrees of freedom",
>      ylab = "Standard deviation of correlations")
>
>
> However, I continue to think that increasing the shape parameter of a LKJ distribution (starting at eta = 1 -> joint uniform) is more intuitive than increasing the degrees of freedom of an inverse Wishart (starting at d = k + 1 -> no moments) in part because the "degrees of freedom" is kind of a nondescript number, while the LKJ correlation matrix is a composition of independent symmetric betas on (-1,1) whose shape parameters are a function of eta.
>

That could be.  You and Bob can explain the LKJ model to me at some stan mtg.

> > Most people don't have a good understanding of joint distributions, correlation matrices, etc. and even if they understand them, they don't have strong priors about correlation matrices, particularly if it is a correlation matrix among parameters rather than data. So, in that situation, a joint uniform distribution on a correlation matrix accurately reflects their prior beliefs.

Maybe.  But there are some settings, especially in high or even moderate dimensions, where a uniform distribution is highly informative along dimensions that matter.  I don't know that this is the case here, but it can come up.

> And insofar as they have informative prior beliefs, they probably slightly favor the identity matrix over the nearly singular correlation matrices, which can be accomplished with an eta slightly greater than 1.0.

Yes, I think this is right but it's hard for me to formalize this notion.  Maybe there's an asymmetric loss, in which we're worse off assuming singularity when the truth is non-singular, than vice-versa.

>
> > A related issue is that in a multilevel model, if you shift the x-variables (for example, by centering them), this changes all the correlations.
>
> Yes, if the correlation matrix in question is among parameters.
>
> > Based on what you're saying here, the uniform on the corrs does seem to make the most sense.  Is there a parameterized version of this (just as the inv-wishart has that df parameterization)?
>
> Yes, what Bob and I call the LKJ distribution over a correlation matrix (with shape parameter eta > ) in stan is based on this paper
>
> http://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=5449838284935626139&hl=en&as_sdt=0,33
>
> which gives conditions under which the PDF of a correlation matrix is
>
> f(Sigma | eta) = 1 / c(k,eta) * det(Sigma)^(eta - 1)
>
> where Sigma is a correlation matrix (and a function of eta) and c(k,eta) only depends on k and eta. And so eta = 1 -> f(Sigma | eta) = 1 / c(k,eta) is constant.
>
> > Also, getting back to the uniform model (which I think was also discussed by Barnard, Meng, and McCulloch), let's think briefly about high dimensions.  I know that earlier I said I'm only interested in d up to 10, but it would be good to understand the limit of very high dimensions, if only to get a sense of what the model is doing.  If d is high, then the joint uniform distribution on the corrs implies a marginal dist on each corr that is concentrated near 0.  There's a conceptual problem with such a model:  imagine you start with two variables, y1 and y2, with a corr rho_12 which has a uniform prior.  Now we add more and more variables:  y3, y4, y5, etc.  If we go with the inverse-Wishart, we're fine, all these models are coherent (although they have other problems, as you've noted!).  But if we go with the joint uniform, then adding y3, y4, y5, etc. has the effect of changing the prior on rho_12.  Which doesn't seem right to me, somehow, that the addition of more variables into the analysis changes the model for an existing variable.  This sort of paradox shoudn't stop us from possibly using the model, but I'd like to have a good way of thinking about it.
>
> I don't think it is a problem with the prior; it is a problem with high dimensions. An earlier paper by Joe
>
> http://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=8483085447913922429&hl=en&as_sdt=0,33
>
> proves that the c(k,eta) term in the PDF when eta = 1 is
>
> c(k) = c(k - 1) * 2^(k^2 - 2 * k + 1) * Beta(k/2,k/2)^(k - 1)
>
> where Beta() is the Beta function. The hypervolume of correlation matrices is c(k), which eventually starts to decrease as Beta(k/2,k/2)^(k - 1) shrinks faster than 2^(k^2 - 2 * k + 1) increases:
>
> k     c(k)
> 2     2.0
> 3     4.934802
> 4     11.69731
> 5     22.53256
> 6     31.11388
> 7     27.85823
> 8     14.87740
> 9     4.411544
> 10   0.682269
>
> So, given that correlation matrices must be positive definite, as k increases, a Bayesian robot should update its beliefs about the correlations to make them closer to zero. In other words, for large k, the set of correlation matrices is small relative to the set of merely symmetric matrices with ones on the diagonal, and the correlation matrices in that set tend to have small off-diagonals. But people are not Bayesian robots and can fall into the trap of thinking that their model stays "the same" as k increases, instead of conditioning their prior beliefs on the known k.

I don't think this is quite right, but I'll have to think furher about how to express my argument about increasing dimensinality.

On Friday, April 6, 2012 10:19:01 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I don't think this is quite right, but I'll have to think further about how to express my argument about increasing dimensionality.

Maybe another way of thinking about it is in terms of Stein's paradox. Suppose you have two standardized variables x and y. You could estimate the correlation between them with the MLE. Then suppose you get K - 2 more standardized variables, so you could form a K by K correlation matrix. Should you change your estimate of the correlation between x and y? Yes, no matter how arbitrarily chosen the other K - 2 variables are. Specifically, the MLE is dominated in expected aggregate loss by many estimators, most of which have the flavor of shrinking toward the mean / median / modal / common correlation estimate. Assuming what you shrink toward is zero, then you should favor something smaller in magnitude than the MLE correlation between x and y. That doesn't mean that it is a better estimate of the population correlation between x and y, even in expectation, but it is better in expected loss aggregated over all K choose 2 correlations. Now all that is for estimates, but if you know it is going to happen with estimates, then your prior should evolve in a similar fashion as K increases.

It seems that having a prior belief about the marginal correlation between any two variables isn't that helpful for forming a joint prior over K choose 2 correlations, even though the margin is the only thing that is easy to grasp. But for K > 3, the union of someone's marginal priors is usually inadmissible for a correlation matrix, so what good are the marginal priors? I suppose you could have a prior about the marginal correlation between x and y and condition on that when building up the joint prior. That can be handled in the LKJ framework but conditioning on more than one margin gets tedious and introduces the possibility that the joint is impossible.

Ben

On Mon, Apr 2, 2012 at 6:43 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>
>
> On 4/2/12 6:17 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>>
>> On Monday, April 2, 2012 6:09:37 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>
>>    The key to using less space in the compiler is
>>    cutting down on the size of our translation units.
>>
>> Don't totally understand but am all in favor of using less RAM. A
>> complimentary route might be to figure out why clang++ uses a fraction
>> of the RAM that g++ or especially mingw use and maybe there is a way to
>> hint the compiler in the right direction?
>
>
> Let me try to explain.
>
> C and C++ compilation involves two stages:
>
>  1.  Building one or more relocatable object files (.o)
>
>      > clang++ -c foo.cpp
>      > ls foo.o
>
>      > clang++ -c bar.cpp
>      > ls bar.o
>
>  2.  Linking the relocatable object files into an executable:
>
>      > clang++ foo.o bar.o -o myprog
>      > ls myprog
>
> The unit through which a relocatable object file is
> built is called a "translation unit".  In the first
> example, that's the contents of "foo.cpp", with all of
> the (recursive) includes folded in.   In the second, it's
> the same for "bar.cpp".
>
> Now, to achieve this, we need to split definitions and
> declarations.
>
> A.  Declaration (traditionally in a .h file)
>    int foo(int x);
>
>
> B.  Definition (traditionally in a .c file)
>    int foo(int x) { return x + 1; }
>
>
> In order to generate relocatable object files, we only need
> the declarations of functions/variables on which we depend.
>
> Here's the key:
>
>   In order to link, every function and constant needs to be
>   DEFINED in EXACTLY ONE of the .o files.
>
> Templates mess all of this up.  They're halfway between
> declarations and definitions.  It's only when you specify the
> type for a template that you get a definition (or declaration).
>
> So template libs, like Eigen and Boost, are often what's
> called "header only", meaning that they put the declarations
> and definitions in a single file and everything gets built
> as one big translation unit.
>
> That's what Stan does now.  For instance, the following
> does both the compilation and linking:
>
>   > clang++ baz.cpp -o myprog
>
> but it requires baz to import DEFINITIONS of everything
> it needs (other than the std libs, which presumably get
> linked in as necessary).
>
> The header guards on the .hpp files make sure that each
> item is only defined once.
>
> So what we want to do is break the parser and perhaps
> the models into pieces, one with a declaration, and one
> with a definition.
>
> Because templates don't have a definition until they're
> instantiated, C++ lets you create a third type of file called
> a template instantiation file.  This is usually a .cpp
> file that indicates which instantiations of the templates
> you want.  It then plays the role of the definition file,
> getting compiled separately and then linked in later against
> a .o file compiled by including only the declarations.
>
> The simplest way to understand this in action is to look
> at the example in:
>
>   stan/src/demo/templ_inst_demo
>
> where I provide a very simple textbook example.
>
> - Bob

It's a moot point because we decided not to use them.

The name "precompiled headers" is misleading.  You'd think
it would mean what Matt said, namely precompiled object (.o) files.
But it doesn't.  Instead, it's a way for the
compiler to cache the parsing it does of #includes.
That way, the next translation unit you get to, you can lookup
the parsed form of all the header includes up to the point where
the includes diverge.

We're going to use "explicit template instantiation".  That's
just the template version of separating out a pure
declaration header file from the definition source.  This
will let us compile a bunch of smaller .o files separately
and then link them together.

I'm hoping that's kosher on CRAN -- they don't require
header-only libs, do they?

messages.body_plain:
Ben brings up a very good point.

On 4/9/12 12:21 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
 > ... we should probably standardize on some conventions

 > for when to use std::vector, an Eigen::vector, or an Eigen::Array. Personally, I would say that
 > a function be defined on
 > an Eigen::vector or an Eigen::matrix iff the function is doing matrix algebra such as dot products.

I agree.  That was my original intention.

Does anyone object?  It'll mean moving
Matt's unfolded dot product operation to Eigen
vectors.

The operations like sum() and mean() aren't really
matrix ops per se, but they do take whole ranges of
values.  There's no way to do a sum of a 4-D array
without allowing things like sum() to apply to
array structures.  (We don't have that function now,
but general summation could be added through template
metaprogramming the same way we do general gets.)

It's very easy to add features, but it'll be hard to
take them away once Stan gets into the wild.  That's
one reason I've been trying to put the brakes on new
functionality (the other being that we don't have all
the old functionality cleaned up yet, though I believe
everything's at least working at this point).

But then I see the advantage of having
extra functions for arrays.
The other way to go would be to let them be
assigned or even promoted to each other, which could
also be done, though not my preference.

> Not that we shouldn't have a templated version or else versions for each thing separately, but stan often uses a
> std::vector, an Eigen::vector, or an Eigen::Array interchangeably and arbitrarily.

It's rather like Eigen::Matrix vs. Eigen::Array
that way.

Given that arrays and vectors/matrices are only
interchangeable for some operations (like array access
and sum()) but not for others (most of them, including
assignment), I'd say Stan's data types are more "arbitrary"
than  "interchangeable".

 > And we haven't gotten around to
> standardizing on matrix_v, vector_v, etc.

This doesn't affect the BUGS-like Stan language, but
I do think it's worth keeing our API code clean, too.

You can't do that for templated code, unfortunately.
That was the problem with the other cleaning scheme
we tried (vestigest of which may still be left) -- type
inference wouldn't run through it and we don't want to
make users overdeclare types on function calls.

Without templates, we should use these typedefs, though.
But where do we put them?

We also need to get rid of all the namespace and
file-level includes that are lurking about.

- Bob

Ok, so I've tested the changes and, combined with some changes to multi_normal, have reduced the computation for my multivariate time-series model by more than a factor of 2.  Everything passes the unit tests but before I push this I wanted to check about two changes that I made in the process:

As far as I could see, only multi_student_t and some unit tests relied on this functionality and I've replaced it in multi_student_t with a call to dot_product and updated the unit tests.  Does anyone object to this?  If we really want to be able to treat a 1x1 matrix as a scalar, then perhaps we should include an implicit type conversion?

2. I added solve(A,b) and trisolve(A,b) functions which compute A^-1 b.  I'm not sold on the naming (and strictly speaking I only needed trisolve in the end for the changes to multi_normal), linsolve() instead of solve() would be more consistent with Matlab but I'm not sure that's significant really.

Cheers,
Marcus

 >

Yes, I do!  If I understand you correctly, your
proposed change would fundamentally break our type
inference process.

I believe you're talking about the multiply() function
with signature:

    real multiply(row_vector, vector);

If you change that to return a matrix, then we can't do:

    real x;
    vector(K) y;
    x <- y' * y;

because (y' * y) is now a 1 x 1 matrix.

(Yes, I could change the type promotions so that a 1 x 1
matrix can be demoted to a scalar [or a scalar can be promoted
to a 1x1 matrix], a 1 x N matrix demoted to a row vector,
and an M x 1 matrix demoted to a vector, but I'd really rather
not as it makes the entire system much much more complex when
trying to figure out which function to apply and what its
return type should be.)

> If we really want to be able to treat a 1x1
> matrix as a scalar, then perhaps we should include an implicit type
> conversion?

I've designed this the other way around.  If you really
want your vector products to be a matrix, declare the
vectors as matrices.  That is, you can already do it
all with matrices if you declare them right:

    matrix(1,1) x;
    matrix(K,1) y;
    x <- y' * y;

The only drawback is that matrix(K,1) doesn't support any
vector-specific operations like dot_product because it's not
a vector.

> 2. I added solve(A,b) and trisolve(A,b) functions which compute A^-1 b.

That's great.

Why are there two?

I thought we'd have for matrix m, vector v,

    m \ v  ==  inv(m) * v

and for row vector u and matrix m,

    u / m  ==  u * inv(m)

That'd be two functions

    vector divide_left(matrix m, vector v);

and

    row_vector divide_right(row_vector u, matrix m);

I'm happy to add the syntax linking up the division sign in
the parser/compiler.

> I'm not sold on the naming (and strictly speaking I only needed trisolve
> in the end for the changes to multi_normal), linsolve() instead of
> solve() would be more consistent with Matlab but I'm not sure that's
> significant really.

What's linsolve()?

- Bob

Matlab has two basic ways to solve a linear system.  The "backslash" operators \ (and /) which correspond to functions mldivide and mrdivide for "matrix (left|right) divide".  These operators will do all kinds of magic, including handling non-square matrices in reasonable ways and trying to detect structure in square matrices (symmetry, positive definite, diagonal, triangular, etc) to speed up the solver.  linsolve on the other hand takes a third parameter which describes the properties of the matrix and the function, therefore, uses the specific form of solver implied by those properties.

>         2. I added solve(A,b) and trisolve(A,b) functions which compute
>         A^-1 b.
>
>
>     That's great.
>
>     Why are there two?
>
>
> solve() is for a general square matrix.  trisolve() is for the case that
> A is triangular.

Aha.  Do you implement trisolve by taking a lower or upper
triangular view of the matrix in Eigen?  If so, it should be
well defined for any matrix.  On the other hand, if you'd rather
have it throw a domain error if it gets a matrix which is not
triangular, that would make sense, too.  I don't know if anyone
else has an opinion.

I'm guessing we'll eventually add a triangular matrix data
type, in which case it should just take that as an argument.

>
>     I thought we'd have for matrix m, vector v,
>
>        m \ v  ==  inv(m) * v
>
>     and for row vector u and matrix m,
>
>        u / m  ==  u * inv(m)
>
>     That'd be two functions
>
>        vector divide_left(matrix m, vector v);
>
>     and
>
>        row_vector divide_right(row_vector u, matrix m);
>
>     I'm happy to add the syntax linking up the division sign in
>     the parser/compiler.
>
>
> Right, I believe there had been some email about doing that before.
> I'll rework the code into that form (and add a divide_right) and leave
> changes to the parser to you, as I haven't taken the time to really
> understand what's going on in there.

Perfect.  The Boost Spirit Qi parser is quite the piece
of template lazy evaluation magic combined with some serious
metaprogramming.

The basic idea's that the parser parses down to an abstract
syntax tree, which is then used to generate.  Although the
grammar looks reasonably clean, the details of semantic actions
and type propagation are monstrously complicated.  At least as
complex as Eigen's matrix arithmetic evaluation policies and traits
and linked metaprograms.

Thanks again for being so patient with this crazy, sprawling
system.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
These templating problems do get pretty esoteric
to track down.  It's so tempting, yet so not-quite-there
as a programming tool.  I've been trying to stay away
templating except in cases where we absolutely need it.

The way Marcus did it's pretty cool.  I'm also not
sure exactly what's wrong with it, but I have a couple
of hunches.

For what it's worth, clang++ 2.9 is passing all of our tests.

Have you turned off the c++0x flags?  I'm hoping there
aren't new language features/changes that are going to mess us up
later.  But it'd be nice to know now if that's an issue.

At the very least, we can fix the problem by stepping
back a bit on the templating.

So far, we've only used

   Matrix<T,Dynamic,Dynamic> == Stan matrix
   Matrix<T,1,Dynamic> == Stan row vector
   Matrix<T,Dynamic,1> == Stan (column) vector

and have never tried to template on the Dynamic vs. 1
distinction.

I'm pretty sure we don't want the templated multiply() function
on line 1337 to match except for R1,R2,C1,C2 = Dynamic.
And this template is called out by the error report in clang++ 3.0.
For many of the other cases, we want a different implementation
for efficiency or a real return type.

And does anyone know how Matrix<T,1,1> behaves in Eigen?
I know Matrix<T,1,Dynamic> and Matrix<T,Dynamic,1> have
template specializations (essentially completely independent
classes with the same name at the implementation level)
for row vectors and column vectors.

Just for reference, here's the list of types for
multiply and the binary * operator,
where real is either stan::agrad::var or double
and a mixed var/double op is promoted to a var return type:

(real,real) -> real
(real,vec) -> vec
(real,row_vec) -> row_vec
(real,matrix) -> matrix

(vec,real) -> vec
*(vec,vec)
(vec,row_vec) -> matrix
*(vec,matrix)

(row_vec,real) -> row_vec
(row_vec,vec) -> real
*(row_vec,row_vec)
(row_vec,matrix) -> row_vec

(matrix,real) -> matrix
(matrix,vec) -> vec
*(matrix,row_vec)
(matrix,matrix) -> matrix

This is in the LaTeX doc now, too.

For instance, multiplying (1,Dynamic) by (Dynamic,1)
should return a single var and use a single instance
of dot_product_vv (or _vd or _dv depending on real type).

And multiplying (Dynamic,1) by (1,Dynamic) should
return a matrix where each entry is a multiply object.

Another issue is that we don't want to match
double times double.  It's probably not an issue because
there's a more specific template, but it can get
confusing trying to read the code and figure out what's
going to match.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I should've looked closer at the rest of the file.

The good news is that the core algorithms all look
great and it's just what we want to do.  Marcus took
it all the way through matrix mutiplies.

I'll take a pass over it in the next couple of days
and clean up the templating.  Mostly, we just need
to remove some of the generality, replace some templates
with explicit stan::agrad::var instantiations, and
get rid of some to_var.

On line 569, we shouldn't have a function to take
two double matrices and return a var.  Two doubles
should return a double.  Luckily, we already have that
in stan/math/matrix.hpp, so we just need to specialize
a bit.

I think any calls to the functions starting in
line 585 can be replaced with direct calls to the
dot_product..vari constructors, so we can probably just
get rid of these.

I think we've all agreed (at least Matt hasn't objected
yet) to removing the dot_product implementation for
std::vector.

I see a problem with the min implementation on line 648.
We don't want that to be called for doubles -- that
should just return a double value, not promote to a var.
It won't get called because there's an untemplated definition
for double, but we don't want it to be called for int
values, for instance.  We've been burned by that before when
the promotion type gets ambiguous (call conversion of
int to double or call conversion of int to var).

So we need to take all these functions
and replace the template variable with stan::agrad::var
and return the to_var calls on the return.  At that point,
we can go back to using the typedefs as Ben suggested.
I think that'll go a long way to more readability, too.

By the way, primitive numbers are already assignable
to var through var's implicit constructors for all
the primitive numerical types.  That's where the problem
comes from.  (We need it that way or we couldn't use
agrad::var and double interchangeably the way we do in code.)

Exp() looks good -- I didn't even know it was in there.

Thanks for putting in all this work.  It sounds like a lot,
but this shouldn't be hard to fix.

- Bob

compile errors.  It looks like the c++0x features (at least on RHEL6.2)
aren't quite ready for prime time.  The net upshot of this bug for me is that I now have stan compiling with clang++, which should make my development cycle much faster :)

I too was a bit perplexed by the existence of the
agrad::multiply(matrix_d,matrix_d) agrad::dot_product(vector_d,vector_d)
 functions when I was working on this.  However, there are several tests
 which explicitly rely on this so I left it in assuming that someone had
 a good reason I couldn't see.  I would be happy to remove these variants (and
their corresponding tests) if you think they should go.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: test-bugs
messages.body_plain:
I'm a bit unclear as to what

make test-bugs

is intended to accomplish at the moment.

It seems to me that we should either be fixing the --seed to some constant and testing whether the results are within rounding tolerance to what the results were before or passing --test_grad with a clock seed to see if the model compiles and can iterate once with auto-diff gradients within tolerance of finite-diff gradients.

At the moment, we do neither so it just spends a lot of time drawing a lot of samples from a lot of models and ignoring the output. I can see the value in looking at the stan results and comparing them (with a human) to the BUGS / JAGS results, but that is not going to get done every time someone does make test-bugs.

Or at least the makefile should have command-line options along these lines.

Opinions?

Ben

messages.subject: Erroneous binomial_log tests
messages.body_plain:
So there are a couple tests of binomial_log which fail on 32bit machines.  I tracked them down to tests of the form:

  result = binomial_log(nan,N,prob, errno_policy());
  EXPECT_TRUE(std::isnan(result));

There are a number of these which fail on 32bit.  I think we should actually remove the tests however, as their behaviour is not defined.  The issue is that casting nan or +/-inf to an int has an undefined result so the input that binomial_log is getting in those cases is compiler/system/O level/etc dependent.

If no one objects, I'll go ahead and do this, as these are the only thing preventing test-unit from passing on my 32bit machine.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Wed, Apr 11, 2012 at 2:08 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> I should've looked closer at the rest of the file.
>
> The good news is that the core algorithms all look
> great and it's just what we want to do.  Marcus took
> it all the way through matrix mutiplies.
>
> I'll take a pass over it in the next couple of days
> and clean up the templating.  Mostly, we just need
> to remove some of the generality, replace some templates
> with explicit stan::agrad::var instantiations, and
> get rid of some to_var.
>
> On line 569, we shouldn't have a function to take
> two double matrices and return a var.  Two doubles
> should return a double.  Luckily, we already have that
> in stan/math/matrix.hpp, so we just need to specialize
> a bit.
>
> I think any calls to the functions starting in
> line 585 can be replaced with direct calls to the
> dot_product..vari constructors, so we can probably just
> get rid of these.
>
> I think we've all agreed (at least Matt hasn't objected
> yet) to removing the dot_product implementation for
> std::vector.
>
> I see a problem with the min implementation on line 648.
> We don't want that to be called for doubles -- that
> should just return a double value, not promote to a var.
> It won't get called because there's an untemplated definition
> for double, but we don't want it to be called for int
> values, for instance.  We've been burned by that before when
> the promotion type gets ambiguous (call conversion of
> int to double or call conversion of int to var).
>
> So we need to take all these functions
> and replace the template variable with stan::agrad::var
> and return the to_var calls on the return.  At that point,
> we can go back to using the typedefs as Ben suggested.
> I think that'll go a long way to more readability, too.
>
> By the way, primitive numbers are already assignable
> to var through var's implicit constructors for all
> the primitive numerical types.  That's where the problem
> comes from.  (We need it that way or we couldn't use
> agrad::var and double interchangeably the way we do in code.)
>
> Exp() looks good -- I didn't even know it was in there.
>
> Thanks for putting in all this work.  It sounds like a lot,
> but this shouldn't be hard to fix.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: unit tests vs. regression tests
messages.body_plain:
There are really two kinds of tests we want to run.

1.  Unit tests -- make sure everyhting's working according
to spec.  That's where Ben's reformulated tests for BUGS
models would go -- just check they're getting the gradients
right.

Having this be just "make test" is fine by me.  It is what
a user who builds from source will want to do.  Presumably most
users will never see it one way or the other.

2.  Regression tests (sorry for the confusing name, but that's
what they're called) -- make sure the big functional pieces
still give the right answers in similar or less time.
This was the intent for the BUGS models in that place, but Ben
makes a good point for including them in the unit tests in
a limited capacity.  We'd sort of confused their role.
Eventually, the BUGS models full runs will track that we still
get the right answers and also track timing.

- Bob

> > 3.5) execute model with --seed = 0 and --test_grad, check whether lp__ matches the last known correct value of lp__ and check whether the auto-diff gradient matches the finite-diff gradient
> >
>
> That sounds like a decent check. How would you suggest doing that? Creating an actual unit test? This is a really fragile test, though. If there are any underlying changes in implementation, the final lp__ could be off.

I think it would be good to have stan write the auto-diff gradient and the finite-diff gradient into samples.csv when --test_grad is passed, in addition to lp__. Then if we had a text file in each subdirectory that just contained the last known correct value for lp__, we could check things using R if need be.

> Bob and I were talking about implementing unit tests comparing known values to the estimated values taking into account standard errors, which relies on an effective sample size calculation. This would be done without specifying a seed.

That is certainly worth implementing as part of 4)

> The test-bugs target was supposed to be a target that humans typically would not call. Do you use this target? If so, what are you using the target for?

These days, I have been using it to see if the models parse and compile with various compilers. Or when I accidentally do make test-all instead of make test-unit. Either way, everything past the first sample is useless to me, and even the first sample is not as useful as it could be if we implemented step 3.5 .

Ben

messages.subject: model unit/regression test plan
messages.body_plain:
I think we all agree that we test everything.

(This is just the deliverables, not an actual plan
per se.)

We will test:

1) that the compiler is indeed compilable (bin/stanc)

Yes.

This isn't technically an API test, but we might
as well test it compiles.

2) that each BUGS model is able to be translated through the stanc compiler

Yes.

We don't need stanc for this.  stanc
is just the command line method to call the compiler,
which in turn calls the parser and code generator.
We can do that all programatically without invoking
the stanc executable.

3) that each BUGS model is compilable by the compiler

Yes.

This is halfway between a unit test and regression test.

Because the compiler for the models is relatively slow
and we're talking about dozens of them, I think we
should let that decide us to delegate it to the regression
tests.

3.5) that each BUGS model gives right gradients

Yes.

We can also do without stanc here.  Writing the same
kind of code into the tests also lets us avoid file I/O.
We can also test random seeds.

4) that each BUGS model runs to completion (that is, to 2000 samples)

Yes.

Move from unit tests to the yet-to-be developed
regression (aka functional) tests.  Run to completion
should be split R-hat on 4 chains.

4.5) that each BUGS model gets the right answer

Yes.

As Daniel pointed out, this will take some by-hand work
to get the right answers specified somehow.  CSV is easy to
read and if we put it down in order or with headers like
Stan produces, it should be easy to test.  We also have
the dump format reader.

5.0) that models are no slower this time than baseine

This is where we test time per effective sample size.

- Bob

messages.subject: Mixed type operations
messages.body_plain:
So I was inspired and took another whack at handling the mixed type
operations between var and double Eigen::Matrix types.  I've managed to
succeed at compiling and running the test file that Ben had posted and
pushed the changes to the mixed_type branch.  Most of the changes boiled
 down to types in the gebp_traits specializations.  The other thing that
 I had to do was reimplement gebp_traits::madd.

There is still a
good chunk of work to be done.  I haven't tested anything other than
problem-eigen-agrad.cpp so seeing how other operations fair is clearly
important.  Also, and perhaps more importantly, we need to figure out
how to leverage the new dot_product vari implementation directly.  I
think it has something to do with the packet_traits::size parameter.  It
 may also need to be done differently, as that seems to only handle
fixed packet sizes.  Perhaps we need to implement specializations of
gebp_kernel?

I realized the other day that one big advantage this form of mixed_type handling would have is being able to make use of Eigen's expression templates which are currently getting tossed out every time we convert to an Eigen::Matrix in a call to multiply, add, etc.  Conceivably this could make things run much faster by reducing the number of vars/varis that get created.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Mixed type operations
messages.body_plain:
We really need to check with the Eigen
developers as to whether having is_same<double,var>
makes sense.  The problem I see is that you can
assign a var to a double but not vice-versa.

Strategically, it seems to me that if that was
all that was necessary, they would've done it themselves
for complex values.  (That is, you can assign a double
to a complex, but not vice-versa.)

That's not really changing the Eigen code so much
as adding a template specialization.  We've already done
that for specifying the behavior of var as a scalar.

I'm pretty sure, though don't seem to have convinced
anyone else, that auto-dif is going to be at least
as hard to add as complex.

- Bob

we should probably talk about them.

The problem is that I don't think we have extensive
enough unit tests for matrix auto-dif.  The reason
was that we were just pushing var through templated
ops.  Before I'd trust a change this major, I'm going
to want to put all the relevant unit tests in.

The only way that using the Eigen expression templates
is going to be a win is if we can push the auto-dif
partial evals through them.  The cost of doing auto-dif
badly is way higher than the cost of not using expression
templates (we actually DO use all their experssion templates
internally once things get converted to var).

I'm really wishing we'd done a univariate version of
Stan first.  It would've been done ages ago and I'd
be less uptight about making major changes on the "eve"
of our first release.

- Bob

> So I was inspired and took another whack at handling the mixed type operations between var and double Eigen::Matrix
> types.  I've managed to succeed at compiling and running the test file that Ben had posted and pushed the changes to the
> mixed_type branch.  Most of the changes boiled down to types in the gebp_traits specializations.  The other thing that I
> had to do was reimplement gebp_traits::madd.
>
> There is still a good chunk of work to be done.  I haven't tested anything other than problem-eigen-agrad.cpp so seeing
> how other operations fair is clearly important.  Also, and perhaps more importantly, we need to figure out how to
> leverage the new dot_product vari implementation directly.  I think it has something to do with the packet_traits::size
> parameter.  It may also need to be done differently, as that seems to only handle fixed packet sizes.  Perhaps we need
> to implement specializations of gebp_kernel?
>
> I realized the other day that one big advantage this form of mixed_type handling would have is being able to make use of
> Eigen's expression templates which are currently getting tossed out every time we convert to an Eigen::Matrix in a call
> to multiply, add, etc.  Conceivably this could make things run much faster by reducing the number of vars/varis that get
> created.
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus
>

On Fri, Apr 13, 2012 at 1:34 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> On Friday, April 13, 2012 12:20:02 AM UTC-4, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> > A few last notes.  Multiplication operations are pretty robust, as is addition and subtraction.  I was able to get lu().solve() to work with mixed types as well, but it required a change to Eigen code.  It's necessitated by the overloading of is_same<double,var>.  I'm going to see if I can remove the overloads of is_same and still get things to compile.
>
> Sounds promising.
>
> The is_same<double,var> and is_same<var,double> thing was a hack to to circumvent Eigen asserts like YOU_MIXED_TYPES_AND_SHOULD_EXPLICITLY_CAST. We could change lib/eigen to allow mixed type operations between double and var just like Eigen did for double and complex. Whatever requires the least changes to Eigen is best I guess. Or we could try to do something more general and get it upstreamed.

I've played around trying to remove the is_same<> hack.  Unfortunately, the way they do it with mixing real and complex types is by comparing NumTraits<T>::Real instead of T.  If we define NumTraits<var>::Real to be double the EIGEN_CHECK_BINARY_COMPAT assert passes, but it produces a ton of issues elsewhere, since NumTraits<var>::Real is used in a lot of places which should probably be var and not double.

I've modified EIGEN_CHECK_BINARY_COMPAT to use a new struct can_mix<> instead of is_same<>.  (This may not be 100% right because, as Bob pointed out, we can go double -> var but not the other way around.)  This works pretty well, but there are a lot of other parts of the code base which do not handle mixed types properly.  E.G., triangular_matrix_solver's currently only take one Scalar type.  I suspect there are a number of operations like that which would need to be changed to accommodate mixed types.  Fortunately, it seems that basic operations are all handled so there may not be a huge amount of work to do for our uses.

Cheers,
Marcus

The folks at Eigen are already thinking about this.
Apparently, it already works for products, but not
for sums, etc.

We even put in a feature request that's now on their
bug tracker.

Some refs:

Eigen to-do list:
http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/index.php?title=Todo
Support for complex numbers and mixing complex-real is already pretty good. However, some operations are not vectorized
or fully optimized yet. E.g., complex-real scalar (or coeff wise) products. Complex normalization, etc.

Eigen issue tracker:
http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/bz/show_bug.cgi?id=279
(From Gael Guennebaud)

We should also extend the mixing of types to other operations than products. It
makes perfect sens to add complex to real, or substract scalars and autodiff
variables.

All this information could be provide through a unique:

template<A,B> struct PromoteType { typedef XXX ResulType; };

By default, when A!=B, this class would be empty and we could detect that to
trigger a static assertion.

So this is more like a generalization of our current scalar_product_traits and
generalization of our current static assertions in BinaryOp.

... snip ...

(From Gael Gunnebaud):
That said, we already have a template struct to control the returned scalar
type of mixed products, e.g.:

namespace Eigen{
namespace internal{
template<typename T> struct scalar_product_traits<std::complex<T>, T>
{
   typedef std::complex<T> ReturnType;
};
}
}
