And I thought I was the pickiest person about
terminology.  I want to keep two things distinct (though
I'm apparently not doing a very good job of it):

   1.  The model itself, as defined by the parameters, data
       and joint probability function, and

   2.  The implementation of such in a programming language.

Would you be happier if I replaced "BUGS model" with

   "a statistical model originally implemented in BUGS, later
    translated with slight changes in meaning to an implementation in
    JAGS, and now translated from JAGS to Stan's domain-specific
    programming language".

Stan also lets you code such things directly in C++, so
that would be

   "statistical model originally coded in BUGS,
    later translated with slight changes in meaning to JAGS,
    and now translated from JAGS to C++ with dependencies on
    Stan's C++ API".

:-)

- Bob

with a Frankenstein monster like Perl if you don't
plan ahead for how things are going to be extended.

The big issue on the expressiveness front is Bayesian
non-parametric models.  We haven't thought much at
all about those either for expression or implementation.

( I also checked this in under doc/notes/performance.txt )

I'd like to take these measurements from the command line
rather than through R.

I don't care about 32-bit results.

We probably want to compare cross-platform and
cross-compiler (e.g., Windows/Mac/Linux g++/clang++).

I only care about optimization-level 3 results.  We
should be sure to compile JAGS that way, too.  I remember
there used to be some issue about how some of their
binaries were compiled.

Per-Model Measurements
-----------------------

These are all per-model measurements that could be
scatterplotted.

1.  How long does it take to compile?

This is in some sense only relevant for Stan, because
BUGS and JAGS are compiled.

2.  How long does it take to read in data?

This step is actually linked to the model analysis step
in BUGS/JAGS because it's where they unfold the
loops into a big graphical model and check that the
result is a directed acyclic graph.

Stan will thus read much faster because it's just a pure
read (of course, reading binary files would be
much faster I/O, but I/O is dominated by other factors).

2.  How long does it take to converge from a random initialization?

Equivalently, how long does it take to get 1 sample.

Equivalently, how long does it take to get near the posterior mean?

The plan right now is to measure this by how long you have to run
4 chains until the split R-hat on all parameters is less than 1.05.

3.  How long does it take to draw each subsequent effectively independent
sample?

For this, we have to evaluate ESS.  Daniel's implementing
variograms.  I think he'll have some issues to discuss at the
next Stan meeting.

4.  How much contention is there from multiple sampling processes?  Threads?

By this, I mean if we run 4 (or more) sampling processes,
are they fighting over disk access?  Or memory/cache?

This is also tricky to measure because the seek performance
difference between a spinny disk and a SSD is huge.

We can also measure the multi-threaded version of Stan here,
which will require less memory.

We can also think about just buffering all the sample data,
which is almost always possible given the size models we're
dealing with, which makes the sampling fast, but adds a big
write step.  Speaking of which.

5.  How much wait time is there at the end?

None in Stan.  But I seem to recall waiting eons for BUGS and
JAGS programs to actually be done once they'd stopped sampling.
I think this may be because they buffer all the data and then
write it all at once.  (That's a pretty big scaling bottleneck
if you want a lot of samples.)

5.  How much peak memory is required?

Perhaps this can be broken out by stages -- for instance,
Stan might need more memory to compile than run a model
in some cases and the other way around in other cases.  JAGS
might need a lot of memory to analyze and read the model
which can then be freed.

- Bob

messages.subject: extended matrix operations
messages.body_plain:
Everythings working in the parser now for
the folowing cases, but I have a question at
the end about whether to add some more generalized
types.

  elementwise division

  matrix ./ matrix : matrix
  vector ./ vector : vector
  row_vector ./ row_vector : row_vector

and

  elementwise multiplication

  matrix .* matrix : matrix
  vector .* vector : vector
  row_vector .* row_vector : row_vector

and

  matrix division

  row_vector / matrix : row_vector
  matrix \ vector : vector

The matrices here are required to be square
and the first case, have the same number of
cols as the matrix.  To avoid a runtime error,
the matrices need to be square and match the dims
of the vectors, as in:

  row_vector(K) / matrix(K,K) : row_vector(K)
  matrix(K,K) \ vector(K) : vector(K)

(Remember sizes are run-time concepts whereas
matrix vs. vector vs. row_vector is static -- just
like Eigen.)

Should I add the following compile-time signatures

   matrix / matrix : matrix
   matrix \ matrix : matrix

with corresponding run-time checks:

   matrix(1,K) / matrix(K,K) : matrix(1,K)
   matrix(K,K) \ matrix(K,1) : matrix(K,1)

Marcus's code is designed to support this, whereas
I probably would've just hard-coded it all to
the above signatures.  This is really an issue
of where we want type checking and how much we want
to allow matrices to be used like vectors and row
vectors if their dimension sizes are right.

- Bob

Hi gang,

I've been getting frustrated with the long compile times of stan
models, so I spent some time today breaking out a bunch of the Eigen
functionality out of .hpp files and into .cpp files.

The upshot: a logistic regression model that formerly took ~33 seconds
to compile now takes "only" ~12 seconds to compile and link (once the
.cpp files are compiled, which only needs to happen once).

It's a pretty big change in terms of LOC altered, plus the makefile
had to undergo some changes. So before pushing I'd like to check with
Bob and/or Daniel that I haven't done anything catastrophically
stupid. The tests seem to check out, but still good to be safe, and
also we may want to do more of this kind of thing and I don't want to
set any bad precedents.

Matt

My personal take is that any sensible operation or expression should be valid unless there's a good reason not to.  One thing to consider for supporting  matrix(K,K) \ matrix(K,1) : matrix(K,1) (and the RHS variant) is that if someone defines a  matrix(K,D) where D is, e.g., the number of observations.  Do we really want to have a model which compiles and works for everything except D == 1?  Or, alternatively, do we want to force the user to have to construct two different models to handle these cases?

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] extended matrix operations
messages.body_plain:
I think I muddied matters with my notation.
Sorry if the explanation is redundant.

Eigen treats the Dynamic vs. 1 decision in the
template as a compile-time decision and sizing
as a run-time concept (We're not using any other
static sizes, but Eigen supports some other small
fixed sizes, too).

Stan's programming language types line up one-to-one with
the Eigen static template instantiations:

   vector      Matrix<double, Dynamic, 1>
   row_vector  Matrix<double, 1,       Dynamic>
   matrix      Matrix<double, Dynamic, Dynamic>

The two vector types are template specializations of
the matrix type that have special vector-only operations
defined for them.

When I wrote vector(K) and matrix(M,N), what I meant
was dynamic sizing of (K) and (M,N), as in the
C++ variable declaration:

   Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic> A(M,N);

This resolves to the matrix type staticially, with
sizes M and N determined dynamically.
There's no problem here if M and/or N are equal to 1.

Size information for Dynamic indices is checked at
run time (i.e., dynamically).

The version I added to the Stan programming language was:

   matrix(K,K) \ vector(K) : vector(K)

The argument on the right needs to be a vector(K) in
order to infer the result is a vector(K) -- type inference
is all static.  We can check that the left arg is a matrix
and right arg is a vector statically, but we can only
check the dimension matches dynamically at run time.

My question was whether to support matrix static
types with run-time sizing requirements as:

   matrix(K,K) \ matrix(K,N) : matrix(K,N)

The only reason not to do this is if the operation doesn't
make sense, but I think it does make sense.  I just don't know
if anyone ever uses it.  If no one will ever use it, the
argument's to keep things uncluttered.  If people might use
it, we should add it.

If we do have the second form, it'll allow N=1,
but the result will still be statically typed a
as a matrix with one column, not as a (column) vector.

- Bob

>     types with run-time sizing requirements as:
>
>       matrix(K,K) \ matrix(K,N) : matrix(K,N)
>
>     The only reason not to do this is if the operation doesn't
>     make sense, but I think it does make sense.  I just don't know
>     if anyone ever uses it.  If no one will ever use it, the
>     argument's to keep things uncluttered.  If people might use
>     it, we should add it.
>
>
> To cut to the heart of your question, I would say support it then.  It would certainly be helpful if, for instance,
> someone wanted to efficiently implement custom elliptical distributions.

OK -- I added the all-matrix forms for
left and right matrix division and made sure
they compiled in both Stan and that the resulting
C++ compiled.

The way Marcus templated out the division operations
is instructive -- it made this change trivial.

>     If we do have the second form, it'll allow N=1,
>     but the result will still be statically typed a
>     as a matrix with one column, not as a (column) vector.
>
>
> I think that would be the expected behaviour in this case so I don't see a problem.

No problem at all.  It's certainly the documented behavior.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] model builds are broken
messages.body_plain:
You need to add the flags
-Lbin -lstan
to the linker call (assuming that libstan.a has been built by saying
"make bin/libstan.a"). This tells the linker to link against the stan
library. In the makefile, those flags are in the LDFLAGS variable.

If you don't want to use a makefile at all, you can build libstan.a by
hand like so:
g++ -I src -I lib -O3 -g -c -o src/stan/agrad/agrad.o src/stan/agrad/agrad.cpp
g++ -I src -I lib -O3 -g -c -o src/stan/math/matrix.o src/stan/math/matrix.cpp

src/stan/agrad/matrix.o

Matt

messages.subject: Broken build: namespace issues.
messages.body_plain:
One instance of our issue is in src/prob/distributions/multivariate/continuous/inv_wishart.hpp. There is a using statement for stan::math::determinant, defined in src/stan/math/matrix.hpp. The problem is that the stan::agrad::var version of determinant() exists in stan::agrad, defined in src/stan/agrad/matrix.hpp.

The simple solution is not what we want: adding a using statement for stan::agrad::determinant. That will create a dependency from our probability library to the stan::agrad::var objects.

Should we move the src/stan/agrad/matrix.hpp functions into namespace stan::math?

Daniel

PS. I am not sure how this worked before.

messages.body_plain:
On 4/17/12 6:37 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> We shouldn't be calling determinant(S) or determinant(W) there anyway,
> as the underlying Eigen function does not take advantage of the presumed
> positive definiteness of these matrices. Better to call .llt() and get
> the determinant and inverse from L.

Sounds sensible.

Any volunteers to follow Ben's advice?  I'd do it, but
my linear algebra's still too shaky to be trusted
in this setting (unless someone writes all the formulas
out more directly for me -- I'm happy to be the code monkey).

> On Tuesday, April 17, 2012 12:47:05 PM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
>
>     One instance of our issue is in
>     src/prob/distributions/multivariate/continuous/inv_wishart.hpp.
>     There is a using statement for stan::math::determinant, defined in
>     src/stan/math/matrix.hpp. The problem is that the stan::agrad::var
>     version of determinant() exists in stan::agrad, defined in
>     src/stan/agrad/matrix.hpp.
>
>     The simple solution is not what we want: adding a using statement
>     for stan::agrad::determinant. That will create a dependency from our
>     probability library to the stan::agrad::var objects.

Right -- we don't want dependencies from stan::prob to stan::agrad.

The using statement could be added at a higher level if
we stuck to header-only usage, but we're not doing that, either.

So what we need is a template specialization declared in
the instantation file in src/stan/agrad/.

Then, if we import all the headers, argument-dependent lookup
should find the version from the right namespace.

>     Should we move the src/stan/agrad/matrix.hpp functions into
>     namespace stan::math?

That's also OK, but we can't in general have this because
of the std:: functions we implement auto-dif for.

>     Daniel
>
>     PS. I am not sure how this worked before.

All of the header definitions (not just declarations)
were in place for the single translation unit.  At that
point, it's just argument dependent lookup again.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
For the record, I'm pretty certain this is a linker issue and not a namespace issue.  Specifically, it's not finding stan::math::determinant in libstan.a for some reason.  My library foo is weak, however the symbol list

[mbrubake@rincewind bin]$ nm -gC libstan.a | grep determinant
0000000000005590 T stan::math::determinant(Eigen::Matrix<double, -1, -1, 0, -1, -1>)
0000000000000000 W stan::agrad::var stan::agrad::determinant<stan::agrad::var>(Eigen::Matrix<stan::agrad::var, -1, -1, 0, -1, -1> const&)
0000000000000000 W stan::agrad::var stan::agrad::determinant<double>(Eigen::Matrix<double, -1, -1, 0, -1, -1> const&)
0000000000000000 W Eigen::PartialPivLU<Eigen::Matrix<stan::agrad::var, -1, -1, 0, -1, -1> >::determinant() const

suggests that when the .o files are combined together, something different is happening with the stan::math version than the stan::agrad version.  (See the T vs W prefix.)  This is causing the linker to not find the math versions.  I had a theory that this had something to do with the fact that both object files had the same name but playing in that direction didn't yield any results.

About using LLT here, Bob check out multi_normal_log_chol for an idea.  The determinant of a matrix A = L*L^T is the product of the square of the diagonals.  I.E., det(A) = \prod_i L(i,i)^2 or, more stably, log(det(A)) = 2 * \sum_i log(L(i,i)).

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] low-triangular * vector product?
messages.body_plain:
The easiest thing to do is call Stan's multiply().
It will probably be faster than promoting double to var
and calling Eigen's specialized triangular multiply
because of the auto-dif savings.

Better yet would be to write a version of multiply()
for triangular matrices into in agrad/matrix.hpp.
It would have tighter loop bounds and use different
dot_product lengths based on which row you're using
from the matrix.  To avoid promotion, this requires
four implementations ({double,var}*{double,var}).

Longer term, of course, we want to have our
expression template cake and eat it, too.

- Bob

The problem is here (with an identical problem for Wishart):

The new implementation is balking on 1x1 covariance matrices.
(Hat-tip to Daniel for writing such extensive error tests
that they caught this boundary condition.)

For now, I added a test to throw a domain error (or
whatever the policy is) if either Wishart or inverse Wishart
get a 1x1 covariance matrix and changed the unit tests
to match and everything's passing agin.

and it's not being checked, so it must be one of the
linear algebra ops throwing an exception.

Ben -- could you fix it so it works for 1 x 1 matrices?
(There's really not a huge rush on this -- it's just nice
to have everything work in full generality -- it's easier
to doc, for one thing.)

If the (inv_)Wishart is really a generalization of
(inv_)chi_square, we could just call those.

Otherwise, we can add a K=1 case to both distributions' code.

   if (k == 1) {
      // handle 1 x 1 case
   }
   ... rest of code

If the Wishart and its inverse twin are changed
to handle 1x1 matrices we should also have a test
for the values produced on 1x1 matrices if they
are indeed implemented separately in the 1 x 1 case.

Now in BUGS example folder, if the model could not be run in
Stan, I use stan.0 as the file suffix.  In vol3, we have more models
not supported.  I have not figure out what the model is in some of
vol3 examples.  Or because of the discrete parameters in the models,
it is not even tried to implement --- for example, an example is
using the truncated stick-break process to approximate Dirichet process
model, which, I think,  essentially change the problem from non-parametric Bayes
model to parametric model.

Main issues in implemented (or not) bugs examples are:

$ find . |grep stan.0

./vol3/fire/fire.stan.0
./vol2/schools/schools.stan.0
--- it takes NUTS too long to adapt / sample.

./vol3/funshapes/ring.stan.0
./vol3/funshapes/squaremc.stan.0
--- the sampler hangs.

./vol2/ice/vanilla_ice.stan.0
./vol2/ice/pineapple_ice.stan.0
--- we could not specify the joint posterior as BUGS
specifies the model with circles in terms of DAG, which is
not supported by JAGS either.  (Note that JAGS does not
support all functionality of OpenBUGS).

./vol2/t_df/estdof2.stan.0
./vol2/biopsies/biopsies.stan.0

the same model that working, discrete parameters are integrated out.

./vol1/leuk/leuk.stan.0

It is important to essential that make dist create a "tag" for the git HEAD when it creates the tarball for release. Otherwise, it does not get recorded in git's history when there was a release, and it is not possible to do something like

git checkout version_1.0.0

or to git bisect against 1.0.0 or any number of git things that accept a tag as an argument (which is pretty much everything).

It is possible to overwrite an existing tag with the -f option, so make dist could just do something like

git tag -f $(VERSION)
git commit -a -m "made auto-tag"

before taring everything up. But that generates a lot of noise commits when you are just trying to test that make dist is working properly. It might be better to make a script that calls make dist and uploads the tarball and documentation and whatnot and then that script can handle the git stuff at the beginning.

Ben

> > > everything).
> > >
> > > It is possible to overwrite an existing tag with the -f option, so make dist could just do something like
> > >
> > > git tag -f $(VERSION)
> > > git commit -a -m "made auto-tag"
> > >
> > > before taring everything up. But that generates a lot of noise commits when you are just trying to test that make dist
> > > is working properly.
> >
> > I like your following suggestion better for exactly the reason
> > you state above.  That's what we did with SVN for our product.
> >
> >
> > >  It might be better to make a script that calls make dist and uploads the tarball and documentation
> > > and whatnot and then that script can handle the git stuff at the beginning.
> >
> > The danger is that you forget to tag.
>
>
> I'm game for whatever makes sense. Part of me doesn't want a make target to automatically do this since the project is open source and curious contributors could end up tagging builds unintentionally. Scripting sounds good. We could also create a Jenkins project to automate as much as we can, including git tagging, tar-ing, etc.
>
> The other option is to do it manually for the first few releases until we know all the steps involved and then script it.
>
>
>
> Daniel
>
>

And PowerPC with g++ 4.2 won't build libstan or anything else that links against Eigen.

Ben

about the antique enthusiast PowerPC crew.

messages.body_plain:
On Friday, April 20, 2012 3:42:18 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> If a user can't build libstan, they won't be able to compile
> the C++ generated for a model.  But then I'm not too worried
> about the antique enthusiast PowerPC crew.

My main point is that the 2^1 PowerPC users would prevent the 2^x MacIntel users from having a binary version of the rstan package. And the Mac version of R defaults to binary package downloads, so without the binary package, many MacIntel users wouldn't be able to install rstan. If they don't have a C++ compiler, they wouldn't be able to estimate a model, but rstan could check for that and prompt them to install a C++ compiler.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
I'm wondering if the problem with models could be
due to generating object files with double instantations
and then calling with integers.

Could someone with one of the platforms on which
it is crashing try running the version of

  src/models/bugs_examples/vol1/dogs.stan

that I just pushed?  All I did was change the normal
prior parameters to real literals instead of
int literals.

If this fixes the problem, I can fix the code
generator to static cast all the int values to
double values -- I have all that information at the
code-generation point because I have to do type-checking
with integer promotion to double.

It's so cool seeing all these models.  The
100K prior for variance looks really arbitrary
when it's square-rooted to 316!

I also figured out how to do some of the shapes.
They're actually all easy to generate if we only
want to do the forward part of the model.

- Bob

Just a quick note as I'm traveling right now. Try:

clang++ -I src -I lib -O3 -Wall -Wunused-function -g -Wno-tautological-compare -c -o models/bugs_examples/vol1/dogs/dogs models/bugs_examples/vol1/dogs/dogs.o  -Lbin -lstan

Putting the linker statements at the end is necessary for some (most?) compilers.

Cheers,
Marcus

On 4/21/12 4:09 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Saturday, April 21, 2012 3:58:34 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>     Here's the current dot_product in stan/math/matrix.hpp:
>
>     template<int R1,int C1,int R2, int C2>
>     inline double dot_product(const Eigen::Matrix<double, R1, C1>& v1,
>     const Eigen::Matrix<double, R2, C2>& v2) {
>     if (v1.rows() != 1 && v1.cols() != 1)
>     throw std::invalid_argument("v1 must be a vector");
>     if (v2.rows() != 1 && v2.cols() != 1)
>     throw std::invalid_argument("v2 must be a vector");
>     if (v1.size() != v2.size())
>     throw std::invalid_argument("v1.size() must equal v2.size()");
>     return v1.dot(v2);
>     }
>
>     Issue 1
>     -------
>     This only compiles if one of R1 and C1 is 1
>     and one of R2 and C2 is 1, so the dynamic vector checks
>     are redundant (they'll always pass if the code compiled).
>
>
> Things like this are one of the reasons that I favored defining all applicable functions on our typedefs, which hasn't
> gotten done yet. But I agree with everything you said.

Within the Stan programming language, that's
exactly what happens.

Within the API, we've got all sorts of things
going on.

1.  Sometimes there's just a fully-templated
definition in stan/math and nothing in agrad.  And
there's not really a good way to template out the scalar.
The problem is that type inference won't pass through
complex typedefs.

2.  Sometimes (as for dot_product), we have things
fixed for scalar type and then defined in stan/math for
double and stan/agrad for var, but using templates for
Eigen size types.

3.  Sometimes we have everything expanded out for
all of our most specific types.  In those cases, we
can definitely use the typedefs.

I would argue that (3) is the easiest to document and
to understand.  We have more functions to doc, but
no templates winging around.  I think (1) is next simplest
and (2) is most complex to doc and understand.

I think it's a wash for testing purposes.

I'm not sure whether we should just take one approach
and stick to it or decide on a per-function basis.

- Bob

On Sat, Apr 21, 2012 at 8:58 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> I'm writing the dot_self function to get a bit
> more familiar with the templating and wanted to bring
> some coding issues to everyone's attention.
>
> Here's the current dot_product in stan/math/matrix.hpp:
>
>    template<int R1,int C1,int R2, int C2>
>    inline double dot_product(const Eigen::Matrix<double, R1, C1>& v1,
>                              const Eigen::Matrix<double, R2, C2>& v2) {
>      if (v1.rows() != 1 && v1.cols() != 1)
>        throw std::invalid_argument("v1 must be a vector");
>      if (v2.rows() != 1 && v2.cols() != 1)
>        throw std::invalid_argument("v2 must be a vector");
>      if (v1.size() != v2.size())
>        throw std::invalid_argument("v1.size() must equal v2.size()");
>      return v1.dot(v2);
>    }

Are you sure this the latest version you're looking at?  The current version of master doesn't use .dot() but instead uses a dot_product specific varI.

>
> Issue 1
> -------
> This only compiles if one of R1 and C1 is 1
> and one of R2 and C2 is 1, so the dynamic vector checks
> are redundant (they'll always pass if the code compiled).
>
> The reason is that v1.dot(v2) is only defined if both of
> v1 and v2 are Eigen vector template specializations of
> Matrix.  A type Matrix<T,R,C> is a vector template specialization
> if and only if R==1 or C==1.
>
> This means the dynamic checks for row/col size are redundant:
>
>    if (v1.rows() != 1 && v1.cols() != 1)
>        throw std::invalid_argument("v1 must be a vector");
>      if (v2.rows() != 1 && v2.cols() != 1)
>        throw std::invalid_argument("v2 must be a vector");
>
> So I removed them.

This isn't true with the dot_product vari implementation.  Those tests are needed there in that case.

>
> Issue 2
> -------
> The dynamic size match test will throw a std::invalid_argument
> exception.   I'm not sure we want NUTS/HMC to recover form
> this.  Shouldn't we just stop at this point because it indicates
> a programming error?  I can't think of any place this would happen
> where the situation would be corrected with more sampling.

This is up to the caller to determine how to handle.  If the caller wants to, e.g., clean things up before aborting then they should be given the opportunity.

>
>
> Issue 3
> -------
> We're compiling without the -NDEBUG flag, meaning runtime
> assertions are turned on.
>
> If we were to get rid of the size check
>
>     if (v1.size() != v2.size())
>        throw std::invalid_argument("v1.size() must equal v2.size()");
>
> then the call
>
>     return v1.dot(v2);
>
> will cause assertion failure and crash the program.
>
> I think we want to add the -NDEBUG flag back in for speed
> and control the error handling ourselves.  For instance,
> we don't need to check in v.dot(v) for dot_self()!

We probably want to leave those tests in, even with NDEBUG, at least for model compilation as it will catch errors in model specification and potentially produce useful error messages rather than crashing in unpredictable ways.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
A better way to deal with missing data is to
split the data matrix into two:

   data_obs[...]
   data_miss[...]

and then loop over them separately.   You can
then sample the missing data.  But if it's discrete,
you'll have to marginalize them out instead.

The definition of if_else is very simple and it's
hard to see where it could go wrong:

     template <typename B, typename T>
     T if_else(B c, T y_true, T y_false) {
       return c ? y_true : y_false;
     }

So if_else(c,y_true,y_false) should evaluate
to y_true if c != 0 and to y_false if c == 0.
So if data[i] == -1, then data[i] + 1 should be
0.  I'm pretty sure the floating point shouldn't
be going wrong.

The only thing I could think to do here is
instrument if_else and have it print out c
(then remove the instrumentation!).

- Bob

But then I'm still not sure if we want to allow this operation.
It doesn't follow the way Eigen works, and has to resort to
runtime type checking.  (But then even matrix multiplication
has to result to runtime size checking.)

the signature:

>     v1 and v2 are Eigen vector template specializations of

>     if and only if R==1 or C==1.
>
>     This means the dynamic checks for row/col size are redundant:
>
>         if (v1.rows() != 1 && v1.cols() != 1)
>             throw std::invalid_argument("v1 must be a vector");
>           if (v2.rows() != 1 && v2.cols() != 1)
>             throw std::invalid_argument("v2 must be a vector");
>
>     So I removed them.
>
>
> This isn't true with the dot_product vari implementation.  Those tests are needed there in that case.

Right -- see above.  I figured that out as soon
as I removed them and ran the unit tests :-)  That's
why there's nothing checked in yet.

>     Issue 2
>     -------
>     The dynamic size match test will throw a std::invalid_argument
>     exception.   I'm not sure we want NUTS/HMC to recover form
>     this.  Shouldn't we just stop at this point because it indicates
>     a programming error?  I can't think of any place this would happen
>     where the situation would be corrected with more sampling.
>
>
> This is up to the caller to determine how to handle.  If the caller wants to, e.g., clean things up before aborting then
> they should be given the opportunity.

For the API, the caller's just going to get the exception.

What we should really do is add the Boost-type configurable
type checking throughout, but that's a huge pain.

But what I meant was what should the Stan programming
language do --- NUTS or HMC is the caller in that case.

For things like variates out of support, we're throwing
domain error exceptions from inside the densities and
NUTS/HMC treat those the same way as zero probability
cases and reject the parameters.

I'm thinking we want NUTS/HMC to abort when they hit
this kind of problem because they're not going to be
able to sample their way out of it.

>     Issue 3
>     -------
>     We're compiling without the -NDEBUG flag, meaning runtime
>     assertions are turned on.
>
>     If we were to get rid of the size check
>
>          if (v1.size() != v2.size())

>             throw std::invalid_argument("v1.__size() must equal v2.size()");

>
>     then the call
>
>          return v1.dot(v2);
>
>     will cause assertion failure and crash the program.
>
>     I think we want to add the -NDEBUG flag back in for speed
>     and control the error handling ourselves.  For instance,
>     we don't need to check in v.dot(v) for dot_self()!
>
>
> We probably want to leave those tests in, even with NDEBUG, at least for model compilation as it will catch errors in
> model specification and potentially produce useful error messages rather than crashing in unpredictable ways.

We're already trapping the main use of asserts in Eigen,
which are array indices out of bounds.

We definitely want to check at some point rather than
just seg fault.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] if_else function
messages.body_plain:
Here's the definition again:

     template <typename B, typename T>

     T if_else(B c, T y_true, T y_false) {

       return c ? y_true : y_false;
     }

I now realize that this is totally broken.

1.  if c is a var, we need c.val() ? ...
not just c ? ...

2.  if y_true type doesn't match y_false type,
the template matching will fail.  If we generalized
the templates to T1 and T2, then the ternary operator
would fail to match (and we would need to somehow
compute the return type).

I'm going to write the specific cases we care about,
because I can't see how to make templates calculate
the return value properly.  I'd very much like this
to work for int values, so we have:

   int if_else(int,int,int);

It'd be eaiser if everything could get promoted to
double -- then I could use promote_args.  As is, I
can't figure out how to calculate the return type without
writing my own template metaprogram for it or without
a whole lot of code duplication.

First, we need both a regular C++ bool and
a var condition, with the latter calling the former:

   if_else(bool c,   ...) { ... }
   if_else(var v, ...) { return if_else(v.val(),...); }

Then, in terms of the other two args, we need to spell
out seven different implementations:

   (C,int,int) -> int
   (C,,double,int) -> double
   (C,int,double) -> double
   (C,double,double) -> double

   (C,var,T) -> var
   (C,T,var) -> var
   (C,var,var) -> var   [otherwise former two ambiguous]

So that's 14 different functions for this.  And the
API winds up being degeernate because it's only
being defined for int and double.

Am I missing a cleaner way to do this?

- Bob

     template <typename T>
     T if_else(bool c, T y_true, T y_false) {

> time (though we're really looking at only symmetric
> pos def matrices).

Although the asymmetric positive definite matrices almost never come up in statistics, it is probably not good to have a data type of pos_def_matrix that implicitly also requires symmetry. We could have sym_pos_def_matrix but that is a bit long-winded. I'd be happy to stick with cov_matrix in the .stan file if we had a cov_matrix class in the C++ file that could represent a covariance matrix in a myriad of different ways. Then we could parameterize it via the Cholesky factor of the precision matrix without the user really knowing.

> Also, we can mention that users can rescale
> a correlation matrix.  I'll eventually replace
> that transform with the hyperspherical transform
> if it looks like it'll be more efficient.

I worked out that the LKJ and the onion are particular hyperspherical transforms. It is just that they are the only hyperspherical transforms that imply a known joint density for the correlation matrix. You could use another density on the hypersphere(s) and get some correlation matrix, but its joint density would just be (proportional to) the product of the (independent) hypersphere densities times a Jacobian determinant. Hard to see what would be the use of implementing that in stan until someone does it in such a way that the joint density becomes analytically attractive.

Ben

the Cholesky basis of covar matrices using

     stan::agrad::jacobian()

and Eigen's determinant function.  This gives a nice
programmatic way of checking one's work on transforms.

The example for covariance matrix constrining (inverse)
transform is in:

    src/test/prob/transform_test.cpp

The Jacobian calculator in stan::agrad::jacobian() just
applies the Real^K to Real^K function, then runs K
partial derivative propagation passes, resetting the
adjoints in between each pass.

I would say the rule should be: If a function needs some representation of the covariance matrix that is not already present, that function should calculate and cache. That way, we just have to check whether something has been initialized before we use it.

> If we allow general A[m,n] = x;
> assignments, then we can't guarantee positive definiteness.

It's very difficult to allow such assignments in a covariance matrix. We can constrain some product-moment correlations to be zero by constraining the corresponding CPC appropriately, but that isn't implemented yet. Nor do we utilize any sparse matrix operations from eigen. What sort of A[m,n] = x assignments are you contemplating besides x being a block of zeros?

> > I worked out that the LKJ and the onion are particular hyperspherical
> > transforms.
>
> Interesting.  I have to go into Eigen and figure out
> what all the pull() and other ops you used were so I
> can reverse engineer the transform!

All that pull stuff in transform.hpp basically just reflects that fact that we get "K choose 2" CPCs in an Array and need to stuff them into the lower triangle of a Cholesky factor. As in,

L =
1
a x
b e x
c f  h x
d g i  j x

where x is the square root of the sum-of-squares in its row. So, first we pull a:d from the CPCs, and put them in L. Then remark the spot in CPCs that we pull from, pull e:g, and put them in L, etc. And calculate the diagonal values along the way.

The way CPCs work, the i'th row of L turns out to be a (nonuniform) draw on the surface of a hypersphere with i dimensions. If there were another distribution based on the hyperspheres-to-correlations transformation, it would probably be best to make the columns of L.transpose() be the hyperspheres.

> > It is just that they are the only hyperspherical transforms
> > that imply a known joint density for the correlation matrix. You could
> > use another density on the hypersphere(s) and get some correlation
> > matrix, but its joint density would just be (proportional to) the
> > product of the (independent) hypersphere densities times a Jacobian
> > determinant.
>
>  > Hard to see what would be the use of implementing that in
> > stan until someone does it in such a way that the joint density becomes
> > analytically attractive.
>
> I'm just thinking about supporting the corr_matrix data type
> most efficiently in terms of inverse transforms and their
> Jacobians.  The transform only gets applied for initial values.

We already have one function for transforming initial values in transform.hpp called factor_cov_matrix(). It could be based on that.

Ben

messages.subject: no tabs in source, please
messages.body_plain:
Please don't use tabs in C++ source code.

We've gone with an "indent 2" standard for
C++ (mainly because it's the emacs default; I
was used to "indent 4" in Java).

The only files with tabs in them were

    inv_wishart.hpp
    multi_student_t.hpp
    wishart.hpp

There's a simple emacs macro you can use to automatically
convert tabs to spaces on save.

(defun java-mode-untabify ()
    (save-excursion
      (goto-char (point-min))
      (if (search-forward "t" nil t)
          (untabify (1- (point)) (point-max))))
    nil)

  (add-hook 'java-mode-hook
            '(lambda ()
               (make-local-variable 'write-contents-hooks)
               (add-hook 'write-contents-hooks 'java-mode-untabify)))

  (add-hook 'html-mode-hook
            '(lambda ()
               (make-local-variable 'write-contents-hooks)
               (add-hook 'write-contents-hooks 'java-mode-untabify)))

  (setq indent-tabs-mode nil)

Of course, you need to add whichever cpp-mode you're
using.

- Bob

messages.subject: cyclic DAGs and coding BUGS models
messages.subject_clean: cyclic DAGs and coding BUGS models
messages.body_plain:
I'm starting to work through the BUGS models
that still aren't working.

The Jama River Valley model seems like a real hack
with mostly ordered variables with some play in
the middle.  And it's encoded using a cyclic graphical
model.  But I can reduce what's going on to a simple
example for the manual.

BUGS uses cyclic constraints to do things
like select two ordered values in the interval
(low,high), as in:

    a ~ dunif(low,b);
    b ~ dunif(a,high);

It's cyclic because a depends on b and b depends on a.

BUGS will get the wrong joint probability here,
but the conditionals are right, so it presumably
samples correctly.

The right joint probabilty function is:

  p(a,b) = 1/(high - low) * 1/(high - a)

We can code this model in Stan as follows:

   parameters {
     real(low,high) a;
     real(a,high) b;
   }
   model {
      a ~ uniform(low,high);
      b ~ uniform(a,high);
   }

Daniel and I just filled up our board working
out that the transforms produce the right
multivariate Jacobian.

The transform for

    real(L,H) z;

is to take an unbounded z_raw to

    z =  L + (H-L) * inv_logit(z_raw).

Thus the unbounded probabilities work out to:

    p(a_raw,b_raw)

    = 1/(high - low)

      * 1/(high - a)

      * (high - low) * inv_logit(a_raw) * (1-inv_logit(a_raw))

      * (high - a) * inv_logit(b_raw) * (1-inv_logit(b_raw))

The first two terms are for the uniforms and the next two
terms for the transforms.  The first one's redundant when
high and low are data, but not the second one.  The last
two terms give you the Jacobian determinant (the full Jacobian
is lower triangular).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] cyclic DAGs and coding BUGS models
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] cyclic DAGs and coding BUGS models
messages.body_plain:
Yes, I recall that Bugs has an awkward way of expressing constraints.  It's good that we can do this in a cleaner fashion.  This will be a useful contribution of stan.
A

On Apr 26, 2012, at 6:10 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> I'm starting to work through the BUGS models
> that still aren't working.
>
> The Jama River Valley model seems like a real hack
> with mostly ordered variables with some play in
> the middle.  And it's encoded using a cyclic graphical
> model.  But I can reduce what's going on to a simple
> example for the manual.
>
> BUGS uses cyclic constraints to do things
> like select two ordered values in the interval
> (low,high), as in:
>
>   a ~ dunif(low,b);
>   b ~ dunif(a,high);
>
> It's cyclic because a depends on b and b depends on a.
>
> BUGS will get the wrong joint probability here,
> but the conditionals are right, so it presumably
> samples correctly.
>
> The right joint probabilty function is:
>
> p(a,b) = 1/(high - low) * 1/(high - a)
>
> We can code this model in Stan as follows:
>
>  parameters {
>    real(low,high) a;
>    real(a,high) b;
>  }
>  model {
>     a ~ uniform(low,high);
>     b ~ uniform(a,high);
>  }
>
> Daniel and I just filled up our board working
> out that the transforms produce the right
> multivariate Jacobian.
>
> The transform for
>
>   real(L,H) z;
>
> is to take an unbounded z_raw to
>
>   z =  L + (H-L) * inv_logit(z_raw).
>
> Thus the unbounded probabilities work out to:
>
>   p(a_raw,b_raw)
>
>   = 1/(high - low)
>
>     * 1/(high - a)
>
>     * (high - low) * inv_logit(a_raw) * (1-inv_logit(a_raw))
>
>     * (high - a) * inv_logit(b_raw) * (1-inv_logit(b_raw))
>
> The first two terms are for the uniforms and the next two
> terms for the transforms.  The first one's redundant when
> high and low are data, but not the second one.  The last
> two terms give you the Jacobian determinant (the full Jacobian
> is lower triangular).
>
> - Bob
>
messages.body_snippet:
Yes, I recall that Bugs has an awkward way of expressing constraints.  It's good that we can do this in a cleaner fashion.  This will be a useful contribution of stan.
A

Are we talking about in general, or in executables? I'm inclined to
say Stan when talking about the project/package as a whole, but agree
that typing capitals is exhausting. (I get exhausted easily.) Cf.
Matlab the product versus matlab the executable. Or Java the
programming language versus java/javac the command line executable. Or
Google the company versus google.com <http://google.com> and the verb "to google." Etc.

Basically, it seems to me like in prose Stan should get its due as a
proper noun, capital-wise, but that carrying that over to the
computational environment (executable names, CRAN, directory
structures, etc.) is a bit much, since as Andrew mentioned it's a pain
to remember arbitrary (library(RStan)? library(Rstan)?
library(rstan)?) capitalization schemes, and as I mentioned my fingers
get lazy when I'm coding.

However, this is not a position in whose defense I would give up my life.

Matt

allow both!  The reason I wasn't so keen on
"stan" is that it looks terrible in running
text and I've been writing the manual.

All of our running in-text use is caps, including
on the web page and in the doc.

The only executable so far is "stanc".

The C++ namespace is "stan".

The Google Code project name is "stan".

The logo is "STAN".

And we'll go with "rstan" for the official
package name in R, so that'd be library("rstan").
(The problem is that so many packages do this
a different way that any choice is in effect
arbitrary.)
